documents.text: kosslyn, s. m., & hatfield, g. (1984). representation without symbol systems. social research, 1019–1045. @article{kosslyn1984representation, title={representation without symbol systems}, author={kosslyn, stephen m and hatfield, gary}, journal={social research}, pages={1019--1045}, year={1984}, publisher={jstor} } notes --- this paper denounces the rigid bounding of representation and symbolic systems; these representations typically are thought to occur in an internal symbol system that allows the brain to store and use information . this ideas originates from the comparison of brain and computational systems (turing machines). the symbolic approach tries to model cognitive process as symbolic computational problems. in this paper the author reviews many frameworks to model “cognitive process“ specially the brain representational capacity using computational methods beyond the symbolic one. reader: this paper proposes using alternatives method to “symbol systems / von neumann machines” to study" ”cognitive processes” (these other method can be computational manipulating symbols). cognitive science research methods: - functionalism : “brain activity” can be study and understand at the functional level (software) without explicit attention to the hardware (anatomy). the same brain activity / function can be instantiated in different hardware (silicon based / biochemical, etc). - computational model of brain functions. qa: - how the symbols are interpreter with respect to the objects or events in the world that they stand for ? - are neural networks networks symbol systems? i will say yes in the abstract sense, not in the production-system based. - list of brain processes? vision, language, audition, … symbol system def. a symbol system is a system (set of rules / program) that “read“, “interpret“ and manipulates discrete entities called “symbols“. rules + symbols (program + data). the von neumann architecture the basic standard computer architecture: memory, data, cpu, store program. the symbol system was called the “language of thought” . … models of human cognition: cognitive process for this models are programs (rules) that manipules symbols. the author of the paper represent the symbolic methodology in order to model the “visual perception“ process. - anderson and bower’s model of human associative memory. - kosslyn’s model of imagery - newell adn simon’s model of human problem solving symbolic representations symbols are the vocabulary for describing the world. the semantics of symbolic representation is defined in terms of the interpreter (in the eye of the beholder) . the mar project … - theory of computation. - the theory of computation specifies what is computed, not how the computation is actually carried out. the “how“ of the computation is left to the algorithm. - the algorithm embodied in a neural implementation. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cognitive model [simulation of some brain function] - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/graph neural network - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/neuro-symbolic ai - ..

(2018). economic catch-up by latecomers as an evolutionary process. modern evolutionary economics: an overview, 172–207. @article{lee2018economic, title={economic catch-up by latecomers as an evolutionary process}, author={lee, keun and malerba, franco}, journal={modern evolutionary economics: an overview}, pages={172--207}, year={2018}, publisher={cambridge university press} } notes --- catching up dynamics this paper proposes an evolutionary view of economic catch-up, considered a long-run process of closing the gap in capabilities by promoting learning and innovation in interaction with innovation systems (national, sectoral, or regional). one central point that emerges from this perspective is the strong complementarity between domestic firms' learning and capabilities and the national, sectoral, and regional systems in which they operate. if cloning is present early in the catch-up process, and becoming familiar with what firms at the frontier are doing characterizes the first stages of catching up, successful catch-up at later stages may involve doing things differently compared to the leading firms or countries. - immigration - innovation: you just cannot, by definition, beat the front-runner following them; at some point, you have to do things differently (product, process, productivity, ...) - this difference results from the fact that exact copying is almost impossible in practice. knowledge is only partially codifiable and transferable; modifications and adaptations to local conditions are necessary. alexander gerschenkron - 1962 - first theories of catching-up process. strategies of catching up: - imitation - alternative path (ex. electrical vehicles) 2013a - remember, you can combine them; it is not one or the other !!! - buying font-runners companies :) - leapfrogging!!! perspectives on economic catching-up - radical changes in productive practices require a profound transformation of society. - catching-up is the process of learning and building capabilities to master the most advanced model of production. - the production differentiation strategy can diverge from one country to another. - can you catch up only via emulation? no - lee 2013a. - catching up economic literature - peoples and papers. - factors - technological knowledge - ... - innovation: technical, organizational, institutional, ... - failures: - capabilities failures - systems failures - ... a working innovation system must complement domestic firms' learning and capability-building to catch up. - definition of the innovation system on page 4. - what is a market failure? - optimal amount of r&d - - ... catching-up at the firm level ... catching-up at the country level ... catching-up and sectors ... catching-up, sectorial specialization, and leapfrogging ... references - lee, k., & malerba, f. and wu, bochao and lu, chengda and zhao, chenggang and deng, chengqi and zhang, chenyu and ruan, chong and others}, journal={arxiv preprint arxiv:2412.19437}, year={2024} } notes --- index learn: - transformer - attention - rl - … image.png model: - name : deepseek-v3 - type : mixture-of-experts (moe) language model - total parameters : 671 billion (671b) - activated parameters per token : 37 billion (37b) architecture: - multi-head latent attention (mla) : - enhances inference efficiency. - reduces training costs. - previously validated in deepseek-v2 . - deepseekmoe architecture : - optimized for efficient computation and scalability. - also validated in deepseek-v2 . training: - auxiliary-loss-free load balancing : - pioneered by deepseek-v3. - ensures balanced utilization of experts without additional loss terms. - multi-token prediction training objective : - improves model performance by predicting multiple tokens simultaneously. - leads to stronger overall capabilities. - pre-training : - dataset size : 14.8 trillion tokens. - dataset quality : diverse and high-quality. - fine-tuning : - supervised fine-tuning (sft) : tailors the model for specific tasks. - reinforcement learning (rl) : further enhances performance through reward-based training. - efficiency : - training cost : 2.788 million h800 gpu hours. - training stability : no irrecoverable loss spikes or rollbacks during the entire training process. no detail from the paper: fp8 training system , “co-design of algorithms, frameworks, and hardware”, “achieving near-full computation-communication overlap”, …, … we introduce an innovative methodology to distill reasoning capabilities from the long-chain-of-thought (cot) model, specifically from one of the deepseek r1 series models, into standard llms, particularly deepseek-v3. our pipeline elegantly incorporates the verification and reflection patterns of r1 into deepseek-v3 and notably improves its reasoning performance. meanwhile, we also maintain control over the output style and length of deepseek-v3. due to the effective load balancing strategy, deepseek-v3 keeps a good load balance during its full training. therefore, deepseek-v3 does not drop any tokens during training. … introduction list of current models: closed models (openai, anthropic's claude, google gemini); open models (deepseek, llama, qwen, and mistral). auxiliary-loss-free strategy (wang et al., 2024a) for load balancing (wang et al., 2024a) for load balancing, with the aim of minimizing the adverse impact on model performance that arises from the effort to encourage load balancing. deepseek-v3 employs a multi-token prediction training objective , which we have observed to enhance the overall performance on evaluation benchmarks. in order to achieve efficient training, we support the fp8 mixed precision training and implement comprehensive optimizations for the training framework. low-precision training has emerged as a promising solution for efficient training (kalamkar et al., 2019; narang et al., 2017; peng et al., 2023b; dettmers et al., 2022), its evolution being closely tied to advancements in hardware capabilities (micikevicius et al., 2022; luo et al., 2024; rouhani et al., 2023a). as for the training framework, we design the dualpipe algorithm for efficient pipeline parallelism, which has fewer pipeline bubbles and hides most of the communication during training through computation-communication overlap. https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00717 we also develop efficient cross-node all-to-all communication kernels to fully utilize infiniband (ib) and nvlink bandwidths. we meticulously optimize the memory footprint, making it possible to train deepseek-v3 without using costly tensor parallelism. in the first stage, the maximum context length is extended to 32k, and in the second stage, it is further extended to 128k. following this, we conduct post-training, including supervised fine-tuning (sft) and reinforcement learning (rl) on the base model of deepseek-v3, to align it with human preferences and further unlock its potential. during the post-training stage, we distill the reasoning capability from the deepseek-r1 series of models, and meanwhile carefully maintain the balance between model accuracy and generation length. architecture … image.png we first introduce the basic architecture of deepseek-v3, featured by multi-head latent attention (mla) (deepseek-ai, 2024c) for efficient inference and deepseekmoe (dai et al., 2024) for economical training. the basic architecture of deepseek-v3 is still within the transformer (vaswani et al., 2017) framework. deepseek-v3 also adopts mla and deepseekmoe, which have been thoroughly validated by deepseek-v2. compared with deepseek-v2, an exception is that we additionally introduce an auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy (wang et al., 2024a) for deepseekmoe to mitigate the performance degradation induced by the effort to ensure load balance. multi-head latent attention image.png for attention, deepseek-v3 adopts the mla architecture. reader: what is attention? what attention does? how many “attention” instances/implementation are there? references: rope + attention. the core of mla is the low-rank joint compression for attention keys and values to reduce key-value (kv) cache during inference. … basic architecture of deepseekmoe for feed-forward networks (ffns), deepseek-v3 employs the deepseekmoe architecture (dai et al., 2024). compared with traditional moe architectures like gshard (lepikhin et al., 2021), deepseekmoe uses finer-grained experts and isolates some experts as shared ones. auxiliary-loss-free load balancing for moe models, an unbalanced expert load will lead to routing collapse (shazeer et al., 2017) and diminish computational efficiency in scenarios with expert parallelism. conventional solutions usually rely on the auxiliary loss (fedus et al., 2021; lepikhin et al., 2021) to avoid unbalanced load. however, too large an auxiliary loss will impair the model performance (wang et al., 2024a). to achieve a better trade-off between load balance and model performance, we pioneer an auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy (wang et al., 2024a) to ensure load balance. … multi-token prediction inspired by gloeckle et al. (2024), we investigate and set a multi-token prediction (mtp) objective for deepseek-v3, which extends the prediction scope to multiple future tokens at each position. on the one hand, an mtp objective densifies the training signals and may improve data efficiency. … infrastructure deepseek-v3 is trained on a cluster equipped with 2048 nvidia h800 gpus. each node in the h800 cluster contains 8 gpus connected by nvlink and nvswitch within nodes. across different nodes, infiniband (ib) interconnects are utilized to facilitate communications. training framework: the training of deepseek-v3 is supported by the hai-llm framework, an efficient and lightweight training framework crafted by our engineers from the ground up. … fp8 training … image.png - fine-grained quantization - online quantization - … pre-training compare with deepseek-v2, we optimize the pre-training corpus by enhancing the ratio of mathematical and programming examples; while explaining coverage beyond english and chinese. hyper-parameters … model hyper-parameters … we set the number of transformer layers to 61 and the hidden dimension to 7168. all learnable parameters are randomly initialized with a standard deviation of 0.006. in mla, we set the number of attention heads $n h$ to 128 and the per-head dimension $d h$ to 128. multi-head attention (mla) : - number of attention heads ( nh ): 128 . - per-head dimension ( dh ): 128 . - key-value (kv) compression dimension ( dc ): 512 . - query compression dimension ( dc′ ): 1536 . - decoupled queries and keys: - per-head dimension ( dhr ): 64 . feed-forward networks (ffns) : - all ffns, except for the first three layers, are replaced with mixture of experts (moe) layers. - moe layer configuration : - number of shared experts: 1 . - number of routed experts: 256 . - intermediate hidden dimension of each expert: 2048 . - activated experts per token: 8 . - maximum nodes a token can be sent to: 4 . multi-token prediction : - multi-token prediction depth ( d ): 1 . - each token predicts: - the exact next token. - one additional token. additional components : - rmsnorm layers are added after the compressed latent vectors. - scaling factors are applied at the width bottlenecks. model size: - total parameters : 671 billion (671b) . - activated parameters per token : 37 billion (37b) . training hyper-parameters … optimizer & hyperparameters - optimizer : adamw (loshchilov & hutter, 2017) - hyperparameters : - β₁ = 0.9 - β₂ = 0.95 - weight decay = 0.1 training & data details - maximum sequence length : 4k tokens - total pre-training tokens : 14.8 trillion (t) tokens learning rate scheduling 1. warm-up phase : - learning rate linearly increased from 0 to 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ during the first 2k steps . 2. stable learning rate phase : - learning rate kept constant at 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ until the model consumes 10t training tokens . 3. decay phase : - learning rate decays to 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ over 4.3t tokens using a cosine decay curve . 4. final phase (last 500b tokens) : - first 333b tokens : learning rate remains 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ . - last 167b tokens : learning rate switched to 7.3 × 10⁻⁶ . gradient & batch size configuration: - gradient clipping norm : 1.0 - batch size scheduling : - gradually increased from 3,072 to 15,360 during the first 469b tokens . - kept at 15,360 for the remainder of training. parallelism & routing: - pipeline parallelism : - different layers deployed across different gpus . - each moe layer’s routed experts uniformly deployed on 64 gpus across 8 nodes . - node-limited routing : - each token can be sent to at most 4 nodes ( m = 4 ). load balancing & loss configuration - auxiliary-loss-free load balancing : - bias update speed ( γ ): - 0.001 for the first 14.3t tokens . - 0.0 for the remaining 500b tokens . - balance loss weight ( α ): 0.0001 (to prevent extreme imbalance in a sequence). - multi-token prediction (mtp) loss weight (λ) : - 0.3 for the first 10t tokens . - 0.1 for the remaining 4.8t tokens . post-training we curate our instruction-tuning datasets to include 1.5m instances spanning multiple domains, with each domain employing distinct data creation methods tailored to its specific requirements. - reasoning data, - non-reasoning data, - reinforcement learning : we employ a rule-based reward model (rm) and a model-based rm in our rl process. - .. conclusion, limitations, and future directions … references - (2018). talent versus luck: the role of randomness in success and failure. advances in complex systems, 21(03n04), 1850014. @article{pluchino2018talent, title={talent versus luck: the role of randomness in success and failure}, author={pluchino, alessandro and biondo, alessio emanuele and rapisarda, andrea}, journal={advances in complex systems}, volume={21}, number={03n04}, pages={1850014}, year={2018}, publisher={world scientific} } notes --- the provided text outlines the "talent versus luck" (tvl) model , an agent-based simulation designed to quantify the impact of randomness on professional success. while western societies operate under a meritocratic paradigm that rewards personal qualities like intelligence and hard work, the researchers argue that these traits follow a normal distribution while wealth follows a power law . this discrepancy suggests that external factors and "right place, right time" dynamics are the primary drivers of extreme achievement. using computer simulations, the authors demonstrate that the most successful individuals are rarely the most talented, but rather those with average ability and exceptional luck . conversely, highly gifted individuals often fail to reach their potential due to simple misfortune . impact - ultimately, the sources suggest that funding strategies prioritizing diversity and broad resource distribution are more effective than those rewarding past performance, which often confuses luck with merit references - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b pmltdoggy - https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/s0219525918500145.

phenomena related with economic development or the lack of there of. on should strive for change things; the current state of the world is not the only one possible; maintaining a society working is hard let alone improving it. understanding the problems underlying today’s ruling economic theory and resurecting alternatives approaches is a necessary starting point. the phrase "nations did not get civilized to find their industries; they find their industries and later get civilized" is attributed to the economist friedrich list . friedrich list was a 19th-century german economist known for his work on economic development and the role of industries in national development. his ideas emphasized the importance of industrialization as a driver for economic progress and civilization. what was about the ‘market’ that rewards sectors with the same level of productivity so differently? let say a taxi driver in peru vs norway. palleative economic measures instead of profound structural transformation. technological rent , or knowledge-based rent , involves the sale of technological capital to developing countries , which they then use to produce inexpensive goods for export back to wealthier nations. models of economic structural transformation? the human cost of poverty is enourmous. harmony is not the natural state of society. physiocrats: means of “rule of nature“. robert wade : governing the markets. real wages? grounding: - social technique - knowding - action - action organization (abstract construct) - policy, task, guideline, principle, strategy, framework. - social epistemology - study history - economic development as the change of the field - not just metrics of capital accumulation, and efficient allocation of resources. - index note which epistemic goals are pursued by erik s. reinert in how rich countries got rich... and why poor countries stay poor ? the book is not merely an economic history. it is an attempt to reconstruct an alternative understanding of economic development that challenges the dominance of neoclassical economics and comparative-advantage explanations. epistemic goal description stated status --- --- --- explain the origins of national wealth identify why some nations became rich while others remained poor. explicit recover the historical development tradition reconstruct the economic ideas of thinkers from the renaissance through the 19th century that emphasized production, innovation, and industrialization. explicit critique equilibrium economics show the limitations of neoclassical models for understanding development and divergence. explicit explain persistent global inequality account for why international income gaps persist despite globalization and trade. explicit identify mechanisms of increasing returns explain how technological learning, innovation, and industrial specialization generate cumulative wealth. explicit diagnose development failure explain why many poor countries remain trapped in low-productivity activities. explicit reconstruct successful development strategies identify common features of historically successful development trajectories. explicit restore historical realism to economics replace abstract universal models with historically grounded analysis. mostly explicit reveal asymmetries in international trade explain why trade can generate unequal outcomes across countries. explicit develop a production-centered theory of development shift attention from exchange and allocation toward production capabilities and technological upgrading. implicit but central are there any relevant epistemic goals needed to build a better understanding of economic reality that are missing from how rich countries got rich... and why poor countries stay poor ? reinert's framework is powerful but not exhaustive. epistemic goal description why it is relevant? --- --- --- formal causal modeling explicit representation of causal structures and mechanisms. reinert often argues historically rather than formally. quantitative predictive modeling construction of forecasting models. the book explains well but predicts weakly. institutional microfoundations detailed modeling of state, firms, bureaucracies, and incentives. important for explaining variation among industrializers. innovation system modeling formal analysis of national innovation systems. technology is central but not systematically modeled. complexity dynamics explicit treatment of economies as complex adaptive systems. would strengthen cumulative-causation arguments. firm-level capability theory explanation of how productive capabilities emerge inside firms. industrialization ultimately occurs through firms. political coalition analysis modeling how development coalitions form and persist. many development successes depend on political alignment. measurement framework operational metrics for productive sophistication and capability accumulation. necessary for empirical implementation. economic network analysis mapping production and knowledge networks. modern industrial systems are networked structures. computational simulation agent-based or system-dynamics representations. could test hypotheses about divergence and catch-up. what domain epistemic artifact set (desa) results from erik s. reinert's work in how rich countries got rich... and why poor countries stay poor to achieve those goals? the desa generated by reinert's project consists of concepts, distinctions, mechanisms, historical narratives, and diagnostic frameworks. documents.text: rumelhart, d. e., hinton, g. e., & williams, r. j. (1986). learning representations by back-propagating errors. nature, 323(6088), 533–536. ﻿@article{rumelhart1986, author={rumelhart, david e. and hinton, geoffrey e. and williams, ronald j.}, title={learning representations by back-propagating errors}, journal={nature}, year={1986}, month={oct}, day={01}, volume={323}, number={6088}, pages={533-536}, abstract={we describe a new learning procedure, back-propagation, for networks of neurone-like units. the procedure repeatedly adjusts the weights of the connections in the network so as to minimize a measure of the difference between the actual output vector of the net and the desired output vector. as a result of the weight adjustments, internal hidden' units which are not part of the input or output come to represent important features of the task domain, and the regularities in the task are captured by the interactions of these units. the ability to create useful new features distinguishes back-propagation from earlier, simpler methods such as the perceptron-convergence procedure1.}, issn={1476-4687}, doi={10.1038/323533a0}, url={https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0} } notes --- this paper introduces the back-propagation learning procedure, adjusts the weights of the connections in the network to minimize the difference between the actual output vector of the network and the desired output vector. an efficient algorithm for computing gradients of deeply composed functions by propagating error signals backward through the computational graph using the chain rule. qa: - how should backpropagation be conceptualized? what is the correct mental model for understanding the backpropagation algorithm in neural networks? - it’s an optimization method - that takes a computation graph - over problem domain - and adjust the parameters in order to optimize some quality metrics . - … - is the full derivative of the loss function computed? does backpropagation compute the entire derivative of the loss function with respect to all parameters, or only specific components such as gradients with respect to weights and biases? - what is the computational complexity of the back prop method? - why did similar methods already exist for optimizing composed functions? several fields had related techniques before neural network backpropagation: - 1960s – control theory: adjoint state method - 1970s – automatic differentiation: reverse-mode differentiation - optimal control: pontryagin’s maximum principle - numerical optimization: finite-difference gradient estimation - … - - why was backpropagation considered an innovation if related techniques already existed? what specific conceptual or algorithmic contribution made backpropagation important for neural network training? - what exactly were the innovations introduced by the backpropagation algorithm? for example: - efficient gradient computation for multilayer networks - reuse of intermediate derivatives - a recursive error-propagation formulation - what is a gradient? formally, what does the gradient represent in the context of optimizing neural networks? - technical observation set (what can be said about ) pass 1: - weight adjustments - internal representations → hidden units → inner features (represent regularities of the input vector) - internal structure → source problem representation capability - what do we mean by learning representations? why does the perceptron does not learn representations? - what do we mean by an active neuron? … - in this paper; the error is computed wrt activations; then with this info ; … - we need to store the previous weights? - why used the first and not the second derivative? - what does the learning rate represents? - what is “weight space”? - why initialize the network with random weights ? - can we get stuck in “weight space” ? - relation of of weights; internal units vs local minima. - … import math import random import json import time def sigmoid(x): return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-x)) def sigmoid derivative(x): s = sigmoid(x) return s (1 - s) dataset = [ ([0, 0], 0), ([1, 0], 0), ([0, 1], 0), ([1, 1], 1) ] def rand(): return random.uniform(-1, 1) global state latest state = {} stop requested = false # flag for stopping def train network(): global latest state, stop requested # initialize weights w11, w12, w21, w22 = rand(), rand(), rand(), rand() v1, v2 = rand(), rand() b1, b2, b3 = rand(), rand(), rand() learning rate = 0.5 epochs = 20000 # target epochs print(f"training started. connect via browser to monitor.") for epoch in range(epochs): # check stop flag if stop requested: print("training stop requested by user.") break total loss = 0 batch predictions = [] for inputs, y in dataset: x1, x2 = inputs[0], inputs[1] # forward pass z1 = w11 x1 + w12 x2 + b1 a1 = sigmoid(z1) z2 = w21 x1 + w22 x2 + b2 a2 = sigmoid(z2) z3 = v1 a1 + v2 a2 + b3 y hat = sigmoid(z3) # store prediction batch predictions.append({ "input": inputs, "target": y, "output": y hat }) # loss loss = -(y math.log(y hat + 1e-9) + (1 - y) math.log(1 - y hat + 1e-9)) total loss += loss # backpropagation delta3 = y hat - y dv1, dv2, db3 = delta3 a1, delta3 a2, delta3 delta1 = (v1 delta3) sigmoid derivative(z1) delta2 = (v2 delta3) sigmoid derivative(z2) dw11, dw12 = delta1 x1, delta1 x2 dw21, dw22 = delta2 x1, delta2 x2 db1, db2 = delta1, delta2 # update weights v1 -= learning rate dv1 v2 -= learning rate dv2 b3 -= learning rate db3 w11 -= learning rate dw11 w12 -= learning rate dw12 w21 -= learning rate dw21 w22 -= learning rate dw22 b1 -= learning rate db1 b2 -= learning rate db2 # update global state for server latest state = { "epoch": epoch, "loss": total loss, "weights": { "w11": w11, "w12": w12, "w21": w21, "w22": w22, "v1": v1, "v2": v2 }, "predictions": batch predictions } # small delay to prevent cpu lock and make visualization smooth time.sleep(0.02) # loop finished (either completed or stopped) if not stop requested: print("training completed naturally.") else: # send final state update to indicate stopped pass 2. run training train network() references - documents.title: Silberschatz, A., Korth, H. F., & Sudarshan, S. (2011). Database System Concepts.

headings.text: Database Design and the E-R Model
Spatial and Temporal Data and Mobility

documents.text: silberschatz, a., korth, h. f., & sudarshan, s. (2011). database system concepts. @article{silberschatz2011database, title={database system concepts}, author={silberschatz, abraham and korth, henry f and sudarshan, shashank}, year={2011}, publisher={mcgraw-hill education} } notes --- this book explores a data model —the relational model—and its implementations in dbmss. a data model defines what data is and how it can be represented, while a dbms provides the concrete system to store and manipulate data according to that model. why does the relational model prevail—or, more generally, why do data models succeed? because they decouple specification from implementation , allowing data to be represented according to a model while enabling migration across different systems that support the same model. continue here storage and file structure. key questions: - how the dbms represents the database? - how the dmbs operates on that database? - who can access what? - how is the system kept consistent under failures? - how does the system scale? index introduction a database-management system (dbms) is a collection of interrelated data (database) and a set of programs (wrong - a set of subsystems for …) to access those data. a data model conceptual framework that defines mechanisms to represent data , specify operations on that data, and provide a formal semantics that gives a precise meaning to the representations and operations. that is; it provides the semantics of the database ; and guide the implementation of the dbms; that must implement the data model. every data model is suited to different kinds of data — it’s a two-way match between the nature of the data and the capabilities of the model. a data model is conceptually similar to a model of computation in programming language theory — it defines the fundamental structures and operations available for representing and manipulating data. the row data from the domain can be viewed in a different level of abstractions : - physical level – describes how the data is actually stored in the database (files, indexes, blocks, pages). - logical / conceptual level – describes what data is stored and the relationships between them (tables, columns, constraints). - view / external level – describes how data is presented to different users or applications (views, subsets, projections). data model - relational data model – represents data as relations (tables) with tuples (rows) and attributes (columns); operations are based on relational algebra. - entity–relationship (e-r) model – represents data conceptually as entities, attributes, and relationships; often used for database design before implementation. - … properties of relational representation: - normalization – organizing tables to reduce redundancy and avoid update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. - consistency of representation – each relation has a fixed schema with well-defined attributes and value domains. dbms structure - storage manager - query processor - transaction management - … normalization by normalization we mean a non repetitive - and minimal representation; fundamentally - a well decomposed system. a functional dependency is a relationship between two sets of attributes in a relation, where the value of one attribute (or set of attributes) uniquely determines the value of another attribute (or set of attributes). let $r$ be a relation, and let $x$ and $y$ be subsets of attributes of $r$. then: $x \to y$ means that for any two tuples $t 1, t 2 \in r$: $t 1[x] = t 2[x] \implies t 1[y] = t 2[y]$. in words: if two tuples have the same values for attributes $x$, they must have the same values for attributes $y$. introduction to relational model a data model defines what data is and how it can be represented , while a dbms provides the concrete system to store and manipulate data according to that model. relational algebra is a tool to formalize the operations on the objects that represented the data. concepts: - relation: a table representing a set of entities or relationships. each relation has a name and consists of tuples (rows) and attributes (columns). - tuple: a single row in a relation; an ordered set of values corresponding to the attributes. - attribute: a named column in a relation that represents a property or characteristic of the entity. - domain: the set of allowable values for a given attribute. - value: an individual data item from the domain of an attribute; a single element of a tuple. - schema: the structure of a relation, including its name, attributes, and their domains. - key: an attribute (or set of attributes) whose values uniquely identify each tuple in a relation. - constraint: a rule that restricts the data in a relation, such as a key constraint, domain constraint, or referential integrity. introduction to sql a sql statement operation on a set of bags; basically in at least one bag; or relation. data types: … set operations: … parts of sql: - data definition language (ddl): commands that define or modify the structure of database objects, such as create , alter , and drop . - data manipulation language (dml): commands that retrieve or modify data, such as select , insert , update , and delete . - data control language (dcl): commands that manage access and permissions, such as grant and revoke . - transaction control language (tcl): commands that manage transactions, such as commit , rollback , and savepoint . intermediate sql an exploration on joins, views, materialized views, transactions, constraints, authorization. a transaction combine a set of statements into an atomic unit of work; that, it’s transactional. note: a individual basic statement, it’s also transactional. the authorization model defines who can do what in a database system. conceptually, we have a set of objects (tables, views, procedures, etc.) and a set of users or roles that interact with those objects. the dbms enforces these rules automatically, ensuring that all access to database objects complies with the defined authorizations. advanced sql an exploration of store procedures , functions, triggers, recursive queries, prepared statements, window functions, … prepared statements are a database feature that lets you define a sql statement once, send it to the database for parsing and optimization, and then execute it multiple times with different parameter values. - note my understanding is pretty basic — but understanding how long a prepared statement remains valid (e.g., per connection, per session) and how to manage them across different connections or connection pools is an important practical detail. formal relational query language in this chapter, we take the relational data model and develop a formal semantics for it, known as the relational algebra . relational algebra is a formal query language and algebraic system for manipulating relations (tables) in the relational model of data . it defines a set of operators that take one or more relations as input and produce a new relation as output. these operators are closed under the algebra, meaning the result of an operation is itself a relation and can be further composed with other operations. database design and the e-r model note: this is a design tool . the entity-relationship (e-r) model is a conceptual framework that provides a set of constructs to describe a domain of data. the tools it provides are aimed at modeling entities, attributes, and relationships in a way that captures the real-world structure of the domain, facilitating database design and ensuring consistency, clarity, and completeness before implementation in a relational database. relational database design what makes a good database design? how to model temporal data ? this chapters cover a very sophisticated treatment of dependency theory, algorithms to normalized a relation. category ✅ criteria description --- --- --- 📋 requirements understand use cases identify all operations, reports, queries, and business rules the database must support. gather constraints document regulatory, security, and domain-specific rules affecting the design. 🗂 data modeling identify entities recognize all real-world objects or concepts represented in the database. define attributes list all relevant properties for each entity and determine their data types. establish relationships map how entities relate (1:1, 1:n, n:n) using er diagrams or similar models. 🧩 normalization 1nf ensure all columns are atomic; no repeating groups or arrays. 2nf all non-key attributes fully depend on the primary key; eliminate partial dependencies. 3nf remove transitive dependencies; non-key fields depend only on the primary key. bcnf (optional) strengthened 3nf; every determinant is a candidate key. 🔒 data integrity primary keys ensure each table has a unique identifier for its records. foreign keys maintain referential integrity between related tables. constraints enforce rules like not null, unique, check to prevent invalid data. ⚡ performance indexing create indexes on frequently queried fields to speed up retrieval. partitioning split large tables logically to improve performance and manageability. query optimization structure tables and relationships to reduce expensive joins and computations. 🌱 flexibility modular design keep tables loosely coupled and logically grouped to accommodate future changes. extensible fields plan for optional fields or additional entities to minimize schema refactoring. 📏 consistency naming conventions use clear, consistent, and meaningful names for tables, columns, and keys. documentation maintain schema diagrams, descriptions, and data dictionaries. 🛡 security access control define user roles and permissions for reading, writing, and modifying data. data protection encrypt sensitive fields and implement auditing where required. 🧰 maintainability simplicity avoid overcomplicated schemas; keep relationships and table structures clear. error handling define defaults, constraints, and validation mechanisms to reduce data errors. functional dependency theory see more in normalization. a functional dependency (fd) is a relationship between two sets of attributes in a relational database. it expresses a constraint that the value of one attribute (or set of attributes) uniquely determines the value of another attribute (or set of attributes). this grounds the process of normalization . the procedure is based on a set of axioms that guide the transformation of a database schema to reduce redundancy and ensure data integrity. these axioms are collectively known as armstrong’s axioms , which include rules such as reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity . additionally, there are related corollaries and rules , like the union rule, decomposition rule, and pseudotransitivity , which are derived from armstrong’s axioms and are used to simplify reasoning about functional dependencies and guide schema decomposition. reflexivity - rule: if $y \subseteq x$, then $x \rightarrow y$. - meaning: every set of attributes functionally determines any of its subsets. augmentation - rule: if $x \rightarrow y$, then $xz \rightarrow yz$ for any $z$. - meaning: adding extra attributes to both sides of a dependency preserves the dependency. transitivity - rule: if $x \rightarrow y$ and $y \rightarrow z$, then $x \rightarrow z$. - meaning: dependencies can be chained together. derived rules these are not axioms themselves but can be derived from armstrong’s axioms: 1. union rule: if $x \rightarrow y$ and $x \rightarrow z$, then $x \rightarrow yz$. 2. decomposition rule: if $x \rightarrow yz$, then $x \rightarrow y$ and $x \rightarrow z$. 3. pseudotransitivity: if $x \rightarrow y$ and $wy \rightarrow z$, then $wx \rightarrow z$. temporal relation modeling temporal relation modeling is the art of capturing snapshots of a domain over time . it involves representing how entities, their attributes, and relationships evolve across different points in time . unlike static data models, temporal models allow you to track historical changes, current states, and even future predictions within the same framework. application design and development this chapter is not about dbs; is about the used of dbs by programs. storage and file structure indexing and hashing (2024). artificial intelligence, scientific discovery, and product innovation. arxiv preprint arxiv:2412.17866. @article{toner2024artificial, title={artificial intelligence, scientific discovery, and product innovation}, author={toner-rodgers, aidan}, journal={arxiv preprint arxiv:2412.17866}, year={2024} } notes --- this paper studies the impact of artificial intelligence on innovation, exploiting the randomized introduction of a new materials discovery technology to 1,018 scientists in the r&d lab of a large u.s. firm. ai-assisted researchers discover 44% more materials, resulting in a 39% increase in patent filings and a 17% rise in downstream product in- novation. these compounds possess more novel chemical structures and lead to more radical inventions. however, the technology has strikingly disparate effects across the productivity distribution: while the bottom third of scientists see little benefit, the output of top researchers nearly doubles. investigating the mechanisms behind these results, i show that ai automates 57% of “idea-generation” tasks, reallocating researchers to the new task of evaluating model-produced candidate materials. top scientists leverage their domain knowledge to prioritize promising ai suggestions, while others waste significant resources testing false positives. together, these findings demonstrate the potential of ai-augmented research and highlight the complemen- tarity between algorithms and expertise in the innovative process. survey evidence reveals that these gains come at a cost, however, as 82% of scientists report reduced satisfaction with their work due to decreased creativity and skill underutilization. qa: - can ai in the feature automates testing and i dea selection ? - … references - https://aidantr.github.io/files/ai innovation.pdf - …

documents.text: turing, a. m. (1950). computing machinery and intelligence. mind, lix(236), 433–460. @article{turing1950computing, title={computing machinery and intelligence}, author={turing, alan m.}, journal={mind}, volume={lix}, number={236}, pages={433--460}, year={1950}, publisher={oxford university press} } notes --- [ if it behaves like an intelligence being then it must be intelligent ] the imitation game, proposed by turing, is an early and influential behavioral test for intelligence. rather than defining what it means to ‘think,’ it evaluates whether a machine can successfully imitate a human in conversation. the turing test was a pioneering proposal, but like any evaluative framework, it struggles to account for certain edge cases — particularly those involving non-human or non-verbal forms of intelligence. note: a necessary , but not sufficient, condition for intelligence . index qa - how to measure intelligence ? - does pass this test is a necessary condition to intelligence? does passing this test is a sufficient condition to intelligence? - is this test a great test of intelligence? why? can we pass the test without understanding & being able - can machines think? what is a machine? what is thinking? why this is a b ad question? why creating a statistical survey to find the meaning of thinking is a bad idea? how to answer these questions? - analyzing the uses of word; - [ equivalent & indirect method ] let’s not do it; let’s re-frame the problem instead; with an alternative one; more general and powerful; but that does not address the notion of thinking directly; but implies. - is the imitation test bogus? - chinese room argument: a machine could simulate conversation in chinese without understanding - what happens if every time the interrogator fails to identity the sex? - turing writes the computer strategist possible should be something other than imitates a human. the imitation game setup: three participants are involved: 1. interrogator (c) – a human, in a separate room; 2. subjects - 1. man (a) 2. woman (b) goal: the object of this game is for the interrogator (c) to determine the sex of the participants. the object of b is to help the interrogator (c). rules: - questions: will x please tell me the length of his or her hair? if x is a then x must answer. - the answers must be written; so the voice can’t be use for identification. can machines think? using the above model; now create a behavioral test for intelligence. this setup leads to the following question; what will happens to game with we replace a by a machine? how are the results of the game impacted by that? critique of a new problem note: in this section, turing tries to motivate the usefulness of the question. functional equivalence of the human brain. the problem setting makes clear the different between physical and the intellectual capacities of man. the machines concerned in the game a machine made by a team of human engineers (the description can be known or not (if it’s experimental or accidental)). biological techniques are prohibited due to the likelihood of being able to rear a human being from a single cell. the only machines permitted in the game are digital computers . digital computers the computer behavior if guided by a provided book of rules. the technical name for the book of rules is the “table of instructions”. a digital computer is composed of three parts: - store: …, - executive unit : execute operations, - control : control the execution order of instructions. universality of digital computer aka. laplace machines. 😊 the digital computers considered in the last section may be classified amongst the “discrete-state machines” . how to model any machine as a computer ? are there imaginable digital computers with would do well in the imitation game? contrary views on the main question a set of arguments or objections against the existence of such “thinking machines”. the theological argument thinking is a function of man’s immortal soul. … the “heads in the sand” objection the consequences of machine's thinking would be too dreadful . let us hope and believe that they cannot do so. note: this is not an objection to the possible existence of thinking machines; rather, it is a concern about the potential power of such machines. the mathematical objection there are a number of results of mathematical logic which can be used to show that there are limitations to the powers of discrete-state machines. how the limits of formal systems in mathematics are used to reason about the limits of computation ? the argument from consciousness objection: brain needs feeling. response: if a machine can functionally replicate consciousness or related phenomena in its outputs, then it should be considered equivalent. arguments from various disabilities arguments of the form: “i grant you that you can make machines do all the things you have mentioned, but you will never be able to make one to do x”. lady lovelace’s objection the machine will only perform tasks it has been programmed for, meaning it will not exhibit any emergent behavior. turing did not use 'emergent' here, but the idea that computing the consequences of a given fact is not straightforward; it must be worked out, and surprises may arise. arguments from continuity in the nervous system the nervous system is not a discrete-machine a small error in the information about the size of a nervous impulse impinging on a neuron, may make a large difference to the size of the outgoing impulse. note: turing argues that this did not matter; but i don’t understand. the argument from informality of behavior it is not possible to produce a set of rules purporting to describe what a man should do in every conceivable set of circumstances . the argument from extrasensory perception note: let’s not pay attention to this argument. learning machines why a thinking machine is possible? turing proposes the simulation of brain child ; and then educate that brain. bottom up engineering. turing uses the idea of evolution to think about mind education. turing devices various teaching methods (using a symbolic-logic language / … references - [https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/95-1/papers/125.pdf - https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-test - https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/s11023-020-09549-0 - [ ] https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-room/

documents.text: von foerster, h. (1984). observing systems. notes --- study the relationships that give rise to processes, independent of their physical embodiment—in other words, become a cybernetician. note: to study a new field; first cast a horizontal look of the it. von foerster’s framework has two fundamental principles. - first, we are to understand by cognition the described behavior or a particular class of systems: those which satisfy for their components a specific kind of internal coherance (or eigenbehavior). - we are to understand our own knowledge as resulting from similar kinds of mechanisms. heinz: - use physics to understand complex systems, - try to understand global dynamics, - try to understand cognition index part 1 on self-organizing systems and their environments what is a self organizing system? there is not such as thing as a self-organizing system. an adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. sometimes "adiabatic" is used metaphorically to mean slowly changing , isolated , or without external interference . proof: - let’s assume that such a system exists, assume a finite universe $u$, which is enclosed in an adiabatic shell which separated this finite universe from any “meta-universe’ in which it may be immersed. - assume that in this universe is divided into to parts: one occupied by a self-organizing system $s$, while the other part is occupied by the environment $e$ of $s$ ; so $s \& e = u$. - if it’s organizing, the entropy must decrease $\frac{\delta s i}{\delta t} < 0$, which reads as: the variation of $s i$ with respect to time is negative . that is, as time progresses, the change in entropy must be negative. note: this is not a derivative, it’s an informal notation used to denote small increments. - to be continued. … computation in neural nets molecular bionics memory without record time and memory molecular ethology part 2 perception of future and the future of perception the responsibilities of competence technology: what will it mean to librarians? thoughts and notes on cognition notes on an epistemology of living things object: tokens for (eigen-)behaviors on constructing a reality part 2 publications of heinz von foerster publications by the biological computer laboratory references - von foerster, h. documents.text: wainwright, k., & chiang, a. (2005). fundamental methods of mathematical economics. mcgraw-hill. notes --- the nature of mathematical economics economics uses mathematical models to represent reality, but dismissing them as 'un-realistic' simply because they are models is an unproductive critique . a more meaningful critique focuses on the presentation capabilities of these models and their ability to accurately capture the underlying mechanisms . economic models economic theory is an abstraction of the real world, and it is nearly impossible to describe social systems with complete granularity. therefore, coarse-grained modeling, whether through verbal or mathematical approaches, remains essential in economics. however, with the advent of massive data and advanced computation, we now have the opportunity to refine and enhance these models. variable : an aspect that can change or not about the world. endogenous variables : elements that are in-corportated in the model. exogenous variables : variables outside in our model; that interact. parameter: a component of the modeling framework or meta-model that requires estimation. → unbounded variable; partial model? notation : exogenous variables are denoted with a subscript of $0$; for instance, $p 0$ represents the exogenously determined price. equations can be used to defined things but also assert the equality . equations - … - definitional? - behavioral? equilibrium analysis in economics like many terms in economics, equilibrium is polysemic. however, it can broadly be understood as a constellation of interrelated variables that are so finely adjusted to one another that no inherent tendency to change exists within the model they form. an economic system is in equilibrium when all forces within it are balanced , and no agent has the incentive or ability to change their behavior , resulting in a stable configuration of prices, outputs, and allocations. linear models and matrix algebra comparative statistics and the concept of a derivative rules of differentiation and their use in comparative statistics comparative-static analysis of general-function models optimization models exponential and logarithmic functions the case of more than one choice variable optimization with equity constraints further topics in optimization economic dynamics and integral calculus continuous time: first-order differential equations higher-order differential equations discrete time: first-order difference equations higher-order difference equations simultanous differential equations and difference equations optimal control theory

documents.title: Wittgenstein, L. (2023). Tractatus logico-philosophicus.
documents.text: wittgenstein, l. (2023). tractatus logico-philosophicus. @article{wittgenstein2023tractatus, title={tractatus logico-philosophicus}, author={wittgenstein, ludwig}, year={2023}, publisher={linkgua} } notes --- he took the general character and conditions of representation to be the essence of language, thought, and pictures. what represents a state of affairs in the world must be a state of affairs in the world (a thought or a sentence, for example) and can represent only because it shares a certain structure with what is represented. the “tractatus logico-philosophicus” is a philosophical work by the austrian philosopher ludwig wittgenstein, published in 1921. it is one of the most important and influential philosophical works of the 20th century and is divided into seven main propositions, each exploring different aspects of language, reality, and philosophy. here are some of the main ideas presented in the “tractatus logico-philosophicus”: - picture theory of language and reality: wittgenstein introduces the idea that language functions as a system of representation that mirrors reality. he suggests that meaningful statements (propositions) are like pictures that depict possible states of affairs in the world. this is known as the “picture theory of language,” where language structure corresponds to the structure of reality. - the limitation of language: wittgenstein argues that the limits of language are the limits of our world. language can only represent what can be said about reality; anything beyond that is ineffable or unspeakable. he famously states, “whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.” - the logical structure of propositions: wittgenstein discusses the logical structure of propositions and asserts that the world is made up of atomic facts, which are combinations of objects. propositions are made by using language to represent these facts. he also introduces the concept of logical analysis, where complex propositions can be broken down into simpler components. - the doctrine of the tractatus: wittgenstein proposes that a strict logical structure governs the structure of language and the world. he presents a series of numbered propositions that aim to analyze language and reality, revealing their logical relationships systematically. - reality and the self: wittgenstein addresses the relationship between the self and the external world. he suggests that the self is not an object within the world but is rather the limit of the world. the self is not something that can be represented within the picture of reality. - ethics and aesthetics: while the " tractatus " primarily focuses on logic and language, wittgenstein briefly touches on ethics and aesthetics. he argues that ethical and aesthetic propositions are also expressions of how the world is. still, they cannot be verified or falsified in the same way as empirical propositions. - mystical and metaphysical aspects: toward the end of the “tractatus,” wittgenstein suggests that some philosophical issues arise from misunderstandings of the limits of language. he alludes to mystical and metaphysical aspects, hinting that these aspects can only be understood through non-discursive, intuitive means. it’s important to note that the “tractatus logico-philosophicus” is a complex and dense work open to various interpretations. wittgenstein’s ideas have been the subject of extensive discussion and debate within the field of philosophy, and his later work, particularly his “philosophical investigations,” represents a significant shift in his philosophical views. references tractatus logico-philosophicus a tree diagram that shows the overall structure of the numbering system and propositions tractatus logico-philosophicus (wikipedia.org)

(1985). structure and interpretation of computer programs. mit press. @book{abelson1996structure, title={ structure and interpretation of computer programs }, author={abelson, harold and sussman, gerald jay}, year={1996}, publisher={the mit press} } notes --- a program is a set of interconnected computational elements that animate a computational process . empower the machine and extend its capabilities through programming. programming should be fun—not overly focused on engineering or correctness—but on empowering the machine and making it shine. the work of a programmer is to create a working vocabulary (tool set) to reason & express a solution to a computational problem. reader: naming is crucial for making software understandable, as our associative memory helps us retrieve named objects more easily. note: the terms computation and description of computation are not synonymous. however, the term computation is often used to refer both to a computational process and to its descriptive representation (i.e., the formal specification or generator of that process). this ambiguity should be handled carefully. although usually tolerable in context, it can produce unnecessary linguistic confusion and misleading conceptual impressions. qa: - how to study a programming language ? see the ‘statement space’; type then and see the evaluation result. - … index note - [model of computation] : [description] → generates → [computation] - ( always ask yourself this ) which computation (process) does this model of computation makes easy to describe? - abstract computation → term interpretation - abstract the description of computation - by treading as element - that can be used to build other descriptions. - the idea of a computational entity or program element - to replace the double used of abstraction - and leave the term abstraction only to describe an act. - representational entity - execution entity - what is the nature of some computations? - we control some object (directive interaction) → for this we need a model of the object. - self contain - transformation - design computation (algorithmic) - learned computation - … - how to think about operators - and their properties? - left associative - right associative - (2 + 2) - (3 (4 / 2)) → this expression generates a recursive computation - tree based computation. - remember that computation are ultimately generated by the model of computation implementation . - tree accumulation evaluation strategy (language system level strategy) - the computation generates will be determined: by the description itself - and how the language system - ‘map that description to a computation’. - you have captured the idea that "computation" is a dynamic event generated by static rules (description) operating within a fixed system (model). - computation as an emergent artifact formally, we can think of this in three layers : - description layer : the source code or expression — what you “want” to compute. - mapping layer : the language system/runtime maps the description to a sequence of computational steps (tree, dag, instruction sequence, etc.). - execution layer : the cpu, gpu, or virtual machine executes the computation . here, recursion, parallelism, or dataflow actually manifests - what is a syntactic form (statement type) ? note: each syntactic form has its own evaluation model. - language system evaluation strategy call-by-need (lazy) - call by value (…). - what is tail recursion? perlis: preface every computer program (2tr level model) is a model of a process hatched in our mind; that is itself a model of a real or mental process . a program is a carefully crafted collection of symbols and interconnected functions. as it evolves , driven by changes in our understanding —our mental model of the process—it deepens, expands, and becomes more generalized. on representation note: a universal representation perse does not mean - a from a observer perspective un-structure - if the term universal representation is used to denote a universal mechanism to build representations like json etc - than it has structure and it can be parse and represented by human cognition . if the representation scheme - like ski calculus - yield almost unstructured - hard to parse description - from a human cognitive agent perspective - then this universal mechanism - does not meat the requiremetns of a great representation builder - from the human perspective. note: they are repreesntatios nbuld for machine to machien communicatoin - seems a human did not have to interact with them other evaluation criteira apply to them. problem statement given two approaches to structuring software systems: 1. single data structure + many functions (100 functions over 1 data structure) 2. multiple data structures + fewer functions (10 functions over 10 data structures) decision problem representation - solution space (choices): - $s 1$: single data structure with many functions - $s 2$: multiple specialized data structures with fewer functions - $s 2$: the middle. - evaluation model: - based on principled design criteria , including: 1. expressiveness & simplicity – how well does the structure represent the problem? 2. maintainability & scalability – how easy is it to extend or modify? 3. performance & efficiency – impact on memory usage, caching, and execution speed. 4. reusability & modularity – can the functions and data structures be reused across contexts? 5. cognitive tractability: does this strategy, form, mechanism, and the programs it produces align well with human cognitive capabilities? - trade-offs: - universal representation (single data structure) → more general, potentially more reusable but may lead to inefficient special cases. - specialized representations (multiple data structures) → optimized for specific use cases but may introduce fragmentation and complexity. building functional computational entity building abstractions with functions a computational process is a dynamic entity that exists within a computing system. it unfolds through time, transforming data according to a predefined set of rules. these rules—embodied in a program—govern its evolution, much like the laws of nature shape the physical world. as programmers, our job is to create programs that generate useful processes. a powerful programming language is more than just a way to encoded instructions to the computer. it a framework withing we organize ideas about processes . statement : … combination : a compound expression or statement that builds complexity from simpler elements. operator combination (aka function call / can be an intrinsic function): a combination that is form from a operator, and operants. repl : read-eval-print- loop. black box computational entity (abstraction): expose the interaction interface, not the internals structure. how to enable the change -(addition - subtraction - change) - of computational entities in the system? a function is a description of a modular section of a larger computational process—a structured way to decompose a computation into less granular, well-delimited parts execution path: - recursive - linear - … - generic operations - large scale structure and modularity - object-oriented programming (a system as a society of objects - that send messages to each other). - operations on aggregate (a system like a signal processor). programming language: - which complex computational entities can be built in this language? expression - … - … programming building blocks: - (basic computational entity) primitive expressions (& statements), which represent the simplest entities the language is concern with, - (how to combine computational entity) means of combination (how to create a complex expression), notice that combination = composition. - (how to hide implementation under an interface?) means of abstraction (by which we create an interface (name + …) + to abstract a body); what) (use) / how (details)? - primitives are directly executable . - combinations let you construct structured computation . (larger pieces describing computations) - abstraction lets you encapsulate and reuse logic . names & environment: - naming is the way we refer to things; a basic building block of cognition; but also programming. - name → computational object. - program environment: the memory; the set of name, values asociations. in a programming language; there is fragmentation (scopes). the same name in different scopes can exists. environment (memory) how to reference computational objects ? a set of all program scopes. a name environment is a mapping from a set of names (or variables) to a set of values (or bindings), and it defines how names are associated with their corresponding values within a specific scope . scope - if and , a local environment might be defined for a smaller scope (e.g., a function or block), while a global environment contains all names accessible throughout the program. $n {local} \subseteq n$ $v {local} \subseteq v$ - an environment could be overridden or extended when entering a new scope (e.g., inside a function, a new mapping for a variable might exist). let: - $n$ be the set of all names (variables, functions, or identifiers). - $v$ be the set of all possible values (which could include data types, objects, or functions). - $e$ be the environment , defined as a mapping $e: n \to v$ compound functions function declaration : a mean of abstraction in which a set of statements are given a name. function expression : a syntax form that invokes a function. evaluation in this section - a model of evaluation is provided. how statements are map to values and/or side effects ? operator combinations form a tree expression. evaluating operator combinations can be done using a technique called tree accumulation (percolate value upwards) . syntactic form : refers to the specific structure and arrangement of code elements (such as keywords, operators, and expressions) that conform to the syntax rules of a programming language. evaluating operator combinations: 1. evaluate the operands expressions, 2. apply the function that is denoted by the operator to the arguments that are the values of the operants. the substitution model for function application a simple model of function application; not how the interpreter works. this book will present a model of the interpreter; and then a full interpreter will be built why model an interpreter? it provides a rigorous and formal way to reason about the evaluation process. applicative-order evaluation (eager evaluation) : arguments are evaluated before applying the function, which is used in most imperative languages like c and python. normal-order evaluation (lazy evaluation) : function application happens first, and arguments are evaluated only when needed, as seen in lazy languages like haskell. 1. evaluate the operants expressions, 2. evaluate and apply the function expression to the operants values. ▶️ conditional expressions and predicates predicate : … predicate operator : calling &&, operators is not entirely right because the operants are not always evaluated; the short-circuiting property. predicate synthathic form : … syntathic sugar: syntathic forms that are simply convenient alternative surface structures for things that can be written in more uniform ways are sometimes called syntatic sugar . predicate ? consequent-experssion : alternative-experssion . conditional expression and predicate how to describe conditional computations (or conditional paths)? it’s one the tools to give a computation - … the ability to visualize the consequences of the actions under considerations is crucial to becoming an expert programmer. newton’s method let’s say we want to compute the roots of $y = \sqrt x$ functions and the processes they generate a function is a pattern for the local evolution of a computational process. recursion type: type description canonical case --- --- --- tail recursion recursive call in tail position; no work after the call; optimizable to iteration. accumulator-based factorial; iterative list traversal. linear recursion exactly one recursive call per activation (not necessarily tail). recursive factorial without accumulator. tree recursion each call spawns multiple recursive calls; forms a recursion tree. fibonacci, generating a power set, permutations. mutual recursion two or more functions call each other recursively. even(n) ↔ odd(n) functions. structural recursion recursion follows the inductive structure of input data; guarantees termination. recursing on lists, algebraic data types, ast traversal. generative recursion recursion generates subproblems not structurally present in the input. quicksort partitioning; geometric recursion; fractals. divide and conquer problem is split into smaller subproblems and combined. merge sort; karatsuba multiplication; fft. corecursion (co-recursion) builds potentially infinite structures; defines output by productive unfolding. infinite streams; lazy sequences; generators. primitive recursion restricted form: recursive call on strictly smaller integer; ensures totality. addition/multiplication defined from successor function. higher-order recursion recursion via higher-order combinators or fixpoints. y-combinator; recursive map/fold over higher-order functions. memoized recursion recursion with caching to avoid recomputation; collapses exponential trees. fibonacci with memoization; dp top-down recursion. parallel / concurrent recursion independent recursive branches execute in parallel. parallel merge sort; fork-join divide-and-conquer. backtracking recursion explores search space; unwinds on failure; tries alternatives. dfs with constraint checking; n-queens; sat solvers. continuation-passing recursion recursion expressed by passing continuations; control is explicit. cps-converted evaluator; continuation-based interpreters. metacircular recursion system defined in terms of itself; recursion across meta-levels. a lisp interpreter written in lisp (eval calling eval). formulating abstractions with higher-order functions by abstractions - we mean complex computational elements - that can be used to defined others. … building representational computational entity … building abstraction with data … modularity, objects, and state … metalinguistic abstraction … computing with register machines … references - https://sarabander.github.io/sicp/html/#toc-metalinguistic-abstraction - hume, d. (1990). mathematics: its content, methods and meaning. dorset press. notes --- its content, methods and meaning. this book explores a range of mathematical abstraction concepts, examining their origins, internal logic, and practical applications; demystifying their abstract nature ; and revealing their concrete content . note [(thanks to richard hamming ]: the meaning of abstract mathematical content becomes evident through its use and applications—almost by definition. mathematics, as abstract as it may seem, usually has origins in reality — or can at least be traced back to it. this is why converting highly abstract mathematical ideas into reality-based analogs can be helpful for reasoning and intuition. index qa: - what is the etymology of the word mathematics? what is the form of the earth is to be study; in crystallography the form of crystals. - what is the essential nature of theoretical arithmetic? theoretical arithmetic; is a futher elaboratio of arithmetic; in which we reason over arithmetic as a system independent from reality. the concept of the infinity of those numbers. how to form new numbers? are there more numbers the grain of sands in the from the "xvi century"; its arises from the study of physical processes; in this cases "motion". the idea of motion also give rise to the idea of a "function"; it "phase transition" to a new stage of
