function; to solve problems in geometry, mechanics and alagebra. - which where the origins of differential and integral calculus? newton and liebneiz put the end (to a lot of preparatory works, functions, variables, methods for computing areas, etc) and the beggining to a new discipline; taking functions as the object of it's study. - what is the essense of functional analysis? functional analysis study second-order functions (operators) that take as parameters (functions / functinoals); - tbc: incommensurable magnitudes, the concept of a real number the nature & relation of concretion/abstraction, the nature & relation of continuity/discrete; history of mathematics. - what these abstract mathematical concepts reflect? what is the subject of mathematics? - what is the foundational method of mathematics? - how to explain the significance of mathematics? a general view of mathematics note: exploration of the essential nature of the science. mathematics is the art of creating abstract symbolic systems through the processes of abstraction, generalization , in order to represent systems or processes of interest . these abstract symbolic systems encode properties of elements and their relations in maths, usually the scope of the encoding is only the quantitative or form characterization of elements . central to mathematics is the use of rigorous reasoning and proof to explore and establish truths within these systems. note: we don’t encode elements themselves; just characterizations. mathematical abstractions are generalizations and formalizations through which intuitive concepts—enabling us to represent and understand certain quantitative and qualitative aspects of reality—are encoded within the formal framework of particular branches of mathematics. mathematical abstractions serve as powerful tools in practical life, precisely because they arise as generalized, formal reflections of patterns and structures found in real-world experience. mathematics is a symbolic world with precisely defined rules, in which we construct objects, explore relationships, discover patterns, and derive consequences. however, its purpose is not merely a sterile intellectual game like chess, where the rules are arbitrary and the activity exists only within the game itself. mathematics is grounded in the attempt to represent, understand, and reason about structures that exist in the world: quantities, space, change, uncertainty, information, relationships, and systems. its symbolic constructions become powerful because they reveal deep regularities and invariants that correspond to aspects of reality. the mathematical world is therefore both invented and discovered: we invent the symbolic systems and rules, but we discover the consequences and structures that emerge from them. the value of mathematics lies in the fact that these abstract structures often provide models of real phenomena and allow us to predict, explain, and design systems beyond direct observation. the origins of the mathematical objects - is usually related - to a abstraction - of real objects - like counting numbers - that represent the size of sets. characteristic features: - abstraction : the manipulation of general concepts—such as sets, functions, spaces, and structures—independent of concrete interpretation. this allows for the formulation of theories that apply across various domains by focusing on essential properties rather than incidental details. - axiomatic system : a structured framework built upon axioms —statements assumed to be true—used to derive theorems through formal logic. prominent examples include euclidean geometry , peano arithmetic , and zermelo–fraenkel set theory (zf or zfc) . - proofs : rigorous deductive arguments that establish the truth of mathematical statements within an axiomatic system. proof techniques include direct proof , proof by contradiction , induction , and constructive proof , among others. - formal language : the use of symbolic logic and precisely defined syntax and semantics. mathematical writing minimizes ambiguity through formal definitions, quantifiers (∀, ∃), logical connectives (∧, ∨, ¬, ⇒), and notation standardized across subfields. - structure and generalization : identification of common patterns and structures (e.g., groups, rings, fields, vector spaces) leading to unification of mathematical theories and transfer of results between seemingly unrelated domains. - applications : despite its abstract nature, mathematics is deeply connected to the empirical world. applications range from physics (e.g., differential equations in mechanics), to computer science (e.g., computational complexity), engineering (e.g., control theory), economics (e.g., game theory), biology (e.g., population models), and more. - internal coherence : mathematics values consistency and internal harmony. theories are judged by their elegance , simplicity , and explanatory power . - precision and economy of thought : mathematical concepts are developed to encapsulate maximal content in minimal language. this allows for deep insights to be captured in compact formulations, such as $e = mc^2$ or fermat's last theorem. features of abstraction in mathematics: - quantitative focus : it deals with measurable characterizations and relationships between objects. - hierarchical structure : it forms layers of abstraction, creating systematic hierarchies. - ubiquity : it is present throughout all areas of mathematics. arithmetic (q uantitative property set ) an abstract reference system that emerges from the necessity to characterize collections of objects—fundamentally, their size. later, this reference system was extended to deal with magnitudes, measurements, and other quantitative properties . humans are already born with a basic and evolving sense of numeracy—such as size and length—which forms the intuitive foundation for the abstract reference system. arithmetic is based on the formalization of intuition. this is a general truth for other areas of mathematics; also. number abstraction ladder (aka abstraction path dependency): - words (qualitative) : used to reference or characterize the size of collections (e.g., "many," "few," "some"). - specific numbers (contextual numerals) : symbols typically associated with a particular type of collection or measurement (e.g., "3 apples," "7 days"). - abstract numbers (decontextualized numerals) : general numerical symbols not tied to any specific measurement system or type of collection. the significance of symbols for numbers lies primarily in their ability to embody the concept of an abstract number in a simple and general form. - operations (relational abstraction) : mathematical operations are abstractions of real-world operations or relationships between concrete collections (e.g., combining, partitioning, comparing). quantitative properties: - what is a property? which are the fundamental categories of properties? counting-based (discrete one) - measurement-based (continuous one). geometry (form, space, structure) geometry constitutes an abstract formal system developed for the qualitative and quantitative characterization of spatial form and structure , primarily through the representation of shape, size, and relative position. its structure was progressively generalized to encompass broader spatial relations—such as curvature, continuity, and dimensionality—through extensions of its representational and deductive frameworks. the history of a geometry figure fundamental abstraction in classical geometry is similar to the history of arithmetic. early geometry figure were abstraction from nature figures the moon, etc. problems related to river flooding , grain storage (involving area and volume), and construction were the main practical concerns from which the abstract system of geometr y emerged. in the history of mathematics unification of tree of ideas like application of analitcal methods to geometry has usually generated great success. note: democritus even advanced the notion that geometrical figures consist of atoms of a particular kind . this ideas was very useful in computing the areas and volumes of figures; by dividing them in parts. note: democritus geometric abstraction were very vinculated with the actual abstracted objects; by this taken the idea that nature was atomic; then my figures are also atomic. how to map out arithmetic as a mathematical epistemic framework ? arithmetic is the mathematical epistemic framework for representing, measuring, comparing, composing, decomposing, ordering, and transforming the quantitative aspects of discrete structures . arithmetic answers questions like: - how many? - more or less? - equal? - after adding? - after removing? - repeated how many times? - into how many equal parts? - what remains? these are fundamentally questions about discrete structure . decomposition (epistemic) arithmetic --- --- formal knowledge domain mathematics epistemic framework arithmetic epistemic purpose represent, quantify, compare, and manipulate discrete quantities using well-defined symbolic rules. reality section (target) abstract discrete quantities, counting, numerical magnitude, ratios, and operations over numbers. formal system natural number arithmetic, integer arithmetic, rational arithmetic, decimal positional system primitive objects whole number, number, digit, zero, unit, successor primitive relations equality (=), inequality (<, , ≤, ≥), divisibility, order representation forms numerals, number line, arithmetic expressions, decimal notation, fractions epistemic operators addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, modulus, comparison inference rules associativity, commutativity, distributivity, identity laws, inverse laws, order properties concrete epistemic artifacts 37 + 18 = 55 , 12 × 9 = 108 , gcd(24,36)=12 , multiplication table epistemic process counting → representation → computation → verification → simplification epistemic standards logical correctness, computational correctness, closure, consistency epistemic constraints finite precision, overflow, computational complexity, representational limitations epistemic infrastructure numeral systems, calculators, abacus, spreadsheets, computer arithmetic libraries arithmetic and geometry we use numbers to make measurements and to work with concepts such as volume, area, spatial location, and form. measurement problems lead us to quantities that cannot be captured by natural numbers , prompting us to introduce new types of numbers to account for these gaps. … mathematics of variable magnitudes in the 16th century the investigation of motion was the central problem of physics . through the analysis of motion , a new concept emerged via reflection: the 'variable magnitude.' this marked the origin of a broader conceptual framework, representing a pivotal transition in the history of mathematics. a tipping point where concrete variables like time and distance were made abstract and symbolic. a function is the abstraction of concrete relation between magnitudes . analysis is the branch of mathematics that study functions. references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/history of the function concept - modern mechanics—an indispensable science for new technologies. in this context of world exploration , new science, new technologies was a great environment in which many mathematical problems arises. mathematical analysis is the branch of mathematics that provides the methods (tools) for the quantitative investigation of many processes of change and motion, and of the dependence of one magnitude on another. note: the method of limits if the most relevant concept in analysis . note: the interplay of industry and science is deep - the torricelli experiments was an r&d based experiments; trying to solving a problem in mining industry . case studies: - free fall model, - reservoir modelling, - bernoulli's principle, - torricelli's experiment - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ekdhlza-lwi https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/torricelli%27s experiment key contributors: thinker century key contributions to calculus & analysis --- --- --- isaac newton 17th co-invented calculus (fluxions), laws of motion, infinite series. gottfried leibniz 17th independently developed calculus (notation: $\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\int$, differentials. jacob bernoulli 17th–18th early work on calculus of variations, probability, and exponential calculus. johann bernoulli 17th–18th mentored euler; contributed to optimization and differential equations. daniel bernoulli 18th fluid dynamics (bernoulli’s principle), calculus applications in physics. leonhard euler 18th formalized functions ( $f(x)$), notation ( e, i, $\pi$ ), calculus of variations, series. joseph-louis lagrange 18th–19th calculus of variations, lagrangian mechanics, formalized limits. pierre-simon laplace 18th–19th laplace transforms, celestial mechanics, probability (bayesian inference). carl friedrich gauss 18th–19th differential geometry (theorema egregium), rigorous analysis foundations. augustin-louis cauchy 19th rigorous limits/continuity, cauchy sequences, residue theorem, complex analysis. mikhail ostrogradsky 19th divergence theorem (ostrogradsky’s theorem), integration by parts in $\mathbb{r}^n$. pafnuty chebyshev 19th approximation theory, chebyshev polynomials, probability inequalities. bernhard riemann 19th riemann integral, manifolds (riemannian geometry), complex analysis. karl weierstrass 19th rigorous $\epsilon$-$\delta$ analysis, pathological functions (e.g., nowhere differentiable). henri lebesgue 19th-20th lebesgue integration (modern measure theory), revolutionized real analysis. david hilbert 19th–20th formalized functional analysis, hilbert spaces, foundational work on calculus of variations. john von neumann 20th operator theory, functional analysis, foundational contributions to numerical pdes. andrey kolmogorov 20th theory of distributions (generalized functions), advanced pdes and fourier analysis. laurent schwartz 20th theory of distributions (generalized functions), advanced pdes and fourier analysis. terence tao 20th–21st harmonic analysis, pdes, and additive combinatorics; modern applications of calculus. paul erdős 20th extremal problems, discrete calculus, and combinatorial analysis. terence tao terence tao 20th–21st harmonic analysis, pdes, and additive combinatorics; modern applications of calculus. methods: - infinitesimal analysis : the study of infinitely small quantities, foundational in early calculus, used to describe instantaneous rates of change and cumulative effects, - limits : the method of limits provides a way to compute the value of a quantity through continuous approximation. - analytic geometry : the study of geometry using coordinate systems, unifying algebra and geometry to describe curves, surfaces, and their properties with equations. - differentiation (aka. change differentiation ): computing rates of changes, - integration (aka. change integration ): using the history rates of changes to compute the current state of a system , or the process of summing infinitesimal contributions (such as accumulated changes) to compute quantities like area, volume. - function: … - continuous function, - optimization, - taylor formula, - … vacuum free falling object 1. velocity as a function of time $v(t) = v 0 - g t$ 2. position as a function of time $y(t) = y 0 + v 0 t - \frac{1}{2} g t^2$ reservoir: - a reservoir with a square base of side length $a$ and vertical walls of height $h$ is completely filled with water. what is the total force exerted by the water on one of the vertical walls of the reservoir? analytic geometry … algebra: theory of algebraic equations … ordinary differential equations … partial differential equations … curves and surfaces … the calculus of variations … functions of complex variables … prime numbers … the theory of probability … approximation of functions … electronic computing machines … theory of functions of real variable … linear algebra … non-euclidean geometry … topology … functional analysis … groups and other algebraic systems … qa what is the etymology of the word mathematics? la etimología de la palabra "matemática" proviene del griego antiguo y tiene un significado profundo relacionado con el aprendizaje y el conocimiento. aquí te lo explico: origen griego: - μάθημα (máthema) : significa "lo que se aprende" , "conocimiento" o "estudio" . deriva del verbo μανθάνω (manthánō) , que significa "aprender" . - μαθηματικός (mathematikós) : significa "relacionado con el aprendizaje" o "deseoso de aprender" . evolución del término: 1. en la antigua grecia, "matemáticas" (μαθηματικά) se refería a todas las disciplinas intelectuales , incluyendo la aritmética, la geometría, la astronomía y la música (estas cuatro formaban el quadrivium en la educación medieval). 2. los pitagóricos fueron los primeros en restringir el término al estudio de los números y las formas, dando origen a la matemática como ciencia deductiva. 3. en latín se adoptó como "mathematica" , y de allí pasó a las lenguas romances (español: matemática , italiano: matematica , francés: mathématiques ). curiosidad: - la raíz math- también aparece en palabras como: - polímata (persona con conocimientos en muchas áreas, como leonardo da vinci). - autodidacta (del griego autodidaktos , que aprende por sí mismo). why is mathematics useful? why is mathematics useful? it is a product of self-selection; the development of mathematics is driven by real-life problems and engineering challenges. often, a specific class of problems evolves into a theoretical framework within mathematics. references - aleksandrov, a. d., kolmogorov, a. n., & lavrent’ev, m. a. --- index thinking in general guiding questions: - normative : how should we evaluate our thinking, judgment and decision-making? by what standards? - prescriptive : how do we think? what prevents us from doing better than we do according to normative standards? - prescriptive : what can we do to improve our thinking, judgment, and decision-making, both as individuals and as society? what is thinking? note: this book does not define thinking. how to approach the definition of thinking? how to approach the definition of rationality? note: this book defines rationality as being aware of our best interests in order to achieve our goals. a model of thinking processes: search-inference framework. decision: a choice made from a set of options. decisions are typically guided by the desire to achieve a goal and are based on beliefs about the outcomes of each option. basic types of rational thinking - thinking about decisions, - thinking about beliefs, - thinking about the goals themselves. 🔍 search–inference framework: thinking , is, in its more general sense, a method of finding and choosing among potential possibilities, that is, possible actions, beliefs, or personal goals. chatgpt critisism: 🤡 form over substance this "framework" is not just underdeveloped—it’s conceptually bankrupt. it should be discarded or reworked from the ground up with formal rigor, interdisciplinary grounding, and intellectual humility. 🚫 this framework is crap; we need a more cybernetic framework; todo: design a rigorous decision-making framework—no vague abstractions or lazy generalizations. ✅ - 🧭 possibilities : the set of available choices, possible paths, or candidate answers to the decision problem. - 🎯 goals : the criteria or metrics used to evaluate the desirability or success of different choices. - 🧠 evidence : prior information, observations, or signals that indicate how likely a given choice is to help achieve the stated goals. - ⚖️ judgment : the process of evaluating each choice in light of the available evidence and the defined goals. - 🔎 inference : the active search for relevant and reliable evidence, aimed at improving the quality of judgments and ultimately leading to better choices. ❓ open questions about the search–inference framework - 🎯 how are goals selected? this seems to be one of the most important aspects. how is the problem to be solved even framed in the first place? - ♻️ how do we evaluate and update in real time? how can we continuously revise goals, choices, and judgments as new evidence becomes available? diagnosis : a set of processes aimed at identifying the underlying causes of specific problems. prognosis : an evidence-based estimation of the likely future course, development, or outcome of a condition or system, often following a diagnosis. postmortem (analysis) refers to the systematic investigation conducted after death (or failure) to determine the causes and contributing factors . retrospectiva: del latín retro ("hacia atrás") + specere ("mirar"). knowledge, thinking, and understanding: the book has idiotic takes on this; see my annotation on the book. not all systems has intent; … 1. naive theories - origin: evolve from cognitive biases, incomplete information, or cultural myths. - flaw: resistant to disconfirmation due to lack of falsifiability. - resolution: require evidence-based interrogation (e.g., experiments, counterexamples). 2. understanding - structural analysis: identifying elements and their relationships. example: understanding democracy → institutions, power checks. - functional analysis: - teleological: purpose in designed systems (e.g., democracy → fair representation). - emergent: function without intent (e.g., market equilibrium → supply/demand). - causal mechanism: linking structure to function (e.g., "voting systems → political accountability"). the study of thinking why models and rigorous reasoning? we surveyed all families with six children in a city and documents.text: brandt, l., litwack, j., mileva, e., wang, l., zhang, y., & zhao, l. (2020). china’s productivity slowdown and future growth potential. the world bank. @book{brandt2020china, title={china's productivity slowdown and future growth potential}, author={brandt, loren and litwack, john and mileva, elitza and wang, luhang and zhang, yifan and zhao, luan}, year={2020}, publisher={the world bank} } notes --- thesis : china productivity growth is slowing down. explanation : limited market entry and exit and lack of resource allocation to more productive firms were associated with slower manufacturing total factor productivity growth. earlier reforms led to state-owned enterprises catching up to the private sector productivity levels in manufacturing, but the convergence stalled after 2007. furthermore, the allocation of a larger share of credit and investment to infra-structure and housing led to lower returns on capital, ,a rapid buildup of debt, and higher risk to growth. china’s growth potential remains high, but its long-term growth prospects depend on reversing the recent decline in total factor productivity growth. questions: - what drives productivity growth? - how to reason about the impact of infrastructure? - increased productivity (e.g., improved transport networks reducing time and costs). - economic spillover effects (e.g., better access to services or markets, higher employment). - long-term effects that may not be captured in short-term capital return measures. - how productivity growth is computed? how to measure the increase in productivity ? - how can the contribution of each factor of production to economic growth be calculated? - what is the relation between total factor productivity and labor productivity ? - … productivity: rate of output vs inputs. - intrinsic sectorial productivity - … claims: - china has experienced a marked slowdown in growth in output per worker since the global financial crisis. [economic output / worker] if you fixed the numbers of workers then it means gdp growth decline . - in 2015–18, average gdp growth fell below 7 percent for the first time since 1991, to a large extent due to slowing growth in total factor productivity (tfp) . - aggregate tfp growth slowed from 2.8 percent in the 10 years before the global financial crisis to 0.7 percent in 2009–18. - the process of soes catching up to private sector efficiency has recently stalled. - china’s growth potential remains significant from the perspective of international convergence. - china remains, on average, quite distant from the global technology frontier and thus has substantial remaining potential for catch-up growth. what is the global technology fronteir ? - … data - the data on output (real gdp), employment and the labor share of income (i.e., labor compensation divided by gdp) are from china’s national bureau of statistics (nbs). - the capital stock estimates are from herd (2020) - human capital variable is from penn world table (pwt), (feenstra et al., 2015). - … argumentation capital stock estimates by sector to show that strong investment in infra-structure and housing has been associated with lower returns to capital. [reader. something seems deeply wrong with this arguments - how do we measure the return on infra-structure; in which time frame; can the alternative the local optimal; and infra be global optimal …] in the “ standard growth accounting framework”, growth in output per worker can be allocated into contributions from changes in physical capital, employment, human capital (the education and skills of the labor force), and a residual, total factor productivity. assuming a cobb-douglas production function , output is a function of capital , labor , and tfp , $y = a k^{\alpha} (l h)^{1 - \alpha}$ - y is output, - $a$ is a constant that represents tfp , - $k$ is capital: typically refers to the physical or financial capital used in the production process, - $l$ is labor, - $h$ is human capital represents educational attainment and the return to each additional year of education, - $α$ is a parameter between 0 and 1 that indicates the share of capital in the production function. some simplifications: $\frac{y}{l}$ = $\frac{a k^{\alpha} (l h)^{1 - \alpha}}{l}$ taking logarithms: $\delta \ln\left(\frac{y}{l}\right) = \alpha \left[ \delta \ln\left(\frac{k}{l}\right) \right] + (1 - \alpha) \delta \ln h + \delta \ln a$ growth meta analysis : tian and yu (2012) conduct a meta-analysis of 150 papers and find that the mean aggregate tfp growth is about 2 percent a year after 1978, accounting for about a fifth of gdp growth. china can increase productivity in the service sector. factors behind the recent slowdown in productivity growth reasons: a declining effect of the information and communication technology boom, an aging workforce, slower human capital accumulation, and slowing global trade integration. ??? resource mis-allocation ??? lack of credit, … … china’s still high growth potential there is scope to catch up to global leaders thought the transfer of technology and state-of-the-art management practices. ??? reader. really, is this the recommendation ??? policy recommendations the adoption of more “advanced technology” and “management skills“ from high-income countries, as well as improving the efficiency of resource allocation, can provide a less costly and more certain source of growth over the medium term . market competition and private sector. the policies recomendations are basic improvement; necessary bud local optima . references - china’s productivity slowdown and future growth potential - baumol, w. j., & bowen, w. g. (1965). on the performing arts: the anatomy of their economic problems. the american economic review, 55(1/2), 495–502.%20on%20the%20performin%20151598edb7908029ac16ef0286489254.md) - easy of doing business

(2005). linux device drivers. o’reilly media, inc. @book{corbet2005linux, title={linux device drivers}, author={corbet, jonathan and rubini, alessandro and kroah-hartman, greg}, year={2005}, publisher={o'reilly media, inc.} } notes --- the linux kernel remains a large and complex body of code, however, and would-be kernel hackers need an entry point where they can approach the code without being overwhelmed by complexity. often, device drivers provide that gateway. they are distinct “black boxes” that make a particular piece of hardware respond to a well-defined internal programming interface; they hide completely the details of how the device works. a driver serves as both a model and an abstraction that represents a specific hardware or software system, managing interactions between that system and the rest of the operating system. driver : $d m → d$. it creates a device model; design ethos : mechanism, not policy. write kernel code to access the hardware, but don’t force particular policies on the user, since different users have different needs. driver : a software layer that lies between the applications and the actual device . design technique : modularity or decomposition. linux naming schemes, objects ? … file descriptors … security is a policy issue ; it should be handled by the drivers. firmware : … image.png qa: - how a driver handle concurrent used of a device ? - which abstraction of a device does the driver provide ? - what is the hardware you are driving? - what kind of device is it (e.g., usb, pci, gpio, etc.)? - what protocols does the device use to communicate (e.g., i2c, spi, hid, etc.)? - does the hardware have any special features, limitations, or quirks that need to be accounted for? - initialization : how does the driver detect the hardware? what kernel functions are involved in detecting and registering the device? - communication model : … - buffers and queues : does the driver use circular buffers, dma (direct memory access), or other memory management techniques? - resource management : how does the driver manage hardware resources (e.g., memory, i/o ports, interrupts)? - how does the driver expose functionality to user-space? - what happens when the device is initialized and destroyed? - how does the driver interact with the linux kernel subsystems? - synchronous processing - asynchronous processing - which types of modules does the kernel supports? - how to interpret the results of ifconfig ? - what is a network connection? - what is a connection? - how to list the file system types that a given linux distro supports? - … index an introduction to device drivers some drivers come with a set of tools that provide additional capabilities not integrated within the driver itself. a driver serves as both a model and an abstraction that represents a specific hardware or software system, managing interactions between that system and the rest of the operating system. driver : $d m → d$. design ethos : mechanism, not policy (behavior). write kernel code to access the hardware, but don’t force particular policies on the user, since different users have different needs. driver : a software layer that lies between the applications and the actual device . hardware resource: … resource: … a filesystem type determines how information is organized on a block device in order to represent a tree of directories and files. a file system is not a hardware driver; it’s a software mechanism that provides file abstractions. it’s a second order driver. [file system → disk driver → disk]. it’s quite unusual for a programmer to actually need to write a file system module , because the official kernel already includes code for the most important file system types . file system drivers: - ahci file system driver !!! - ahci (for sata drives) - nvme (for nvme ssds) - scsi (for certain high-performance drives) network interface (hardware / software): - ip link show - ifconfig -a - ls /sys/class/net/ - sudo lshw -c network - nmcli device - sudo ethtool -i enp2s0 - … kernel: - process management: the kernel is in charge of creating and destroying processes and handling their connection to the outside world (input and output). - memory management: the computer’s memory is a major resource, and the policy used to deal with it is a critical one for system performance - file systems: unix is heavily based on the file system concept; almost everything in unix can be treated as a file. - device control (aka driver): almost every system operation eventually maps to a physical device. with the exception to the processor, memory, and a very few other entities, any and all device control operations are performed by code that is specific to the device being addressed. - networking: networking must be managed by the operating system, because most network operations are not specific to a process: incoming packets are asynchronous events. module system (aka plugin system): mechanisms to extend the linux kernel at run time. device models: the linux way of looking at devices distinguishes three fundamental device types. char devices, b lock device, or a network device. others ways to classify drivers usb, scsi, serial modules, … the network devices is the only not stream oriented device; hard to map to the file system . - character devices : a character ( char ) device is one that can be accessed as a stream of bytes (like a file); a char driver is in charge of implementing this behavior. such a driver usually implements at least the open, close, read, and write system calls. the text console ( /dev/console ) and the serial ports ( /dev/ttys0 and friends) are examples of char devices, as they are well represented by the stream abstraction. - block devices : like char devices, block devices are accessed by file system nodes in the /dev directory. they share the fundamental abstraction with char devices . a block device is a device (e.g., a disk) that can host a file system. - network interfaces : any network transaction is made through an interface, that is, a device that is able to exchange data with other hosts. usually, an interface is a hardware device, but it might also be a pure software device, like the loop back interface. - … security considerations: - … versioning numbers: - … building and running modules … char devices … debugging techniques … concurrency and race conditions … advanced char driver operations … time, delays, and deferred work … allocation memory … communication with hardware … interrupt handling … data types in the kernel … pci drivers … usb drivers … the linux device model … memory mapping and dma … block drivers … network drivers … tty drivers … references - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/device driver - https://www.oreilly.com/openbook/linuxdrive3/book/ - https://english.stackexchange.com/questions/56183/origin-of-the-term-driver-in-computer-science - https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/linux/ata.h

"the history of the conquest of the americas was more a political act (pactismo) than a result of superior technology ; therefore, this book is fundamentally mistaken on this point.” macroeconomic history gdp : the total value of all final goods and services produced by a country's residents in a given year. gdp : represents a flow measure , expressed as dollars per year, while wealth is a stock measure , represented as a total dollar amount at a specific point in time. gdp-per-capita-maddison.png image.png gdp measurement strategies how to measure the gdp: method description key features --- --- --- production (or output) method measures gdp by summing the value added at each production stage for all final goods and services. focuses on the production side of the economy; avoids double counting by using value added. expenditure method calculates gdp by summing all expenditures on final goods and services within a country. includes consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports (exports minus imports). income method measures gdp by summing all incomes earned by factors of production, including wages, rents, interests, and profits. reflects the total income earned by individuals and businesses in the economy. gross national product (gnp) measures the total value of goods and services produced by the residents of a country, including income from abroad. includes income earned by residents from abroad and excludes income earned by foreigners within the country. net domestic product (ndp) adjusts gdp by subtracting depreciation (the loss of value of capital goods over time). provides a measure of the economy’s net production capacity after accounting for capital depreciation. real gdp adjusts nominal gdp for changes in the price level, reflecting the value of goods and services at constant prices. allows for comparison of economic output over time by removing the effects of inflation. nominal gdp measures gdp using current prices without adjusting for inflation. reflects the value of goods and services at current market prices. gdp at purchasing power parity (ppp) adjusting gdp to account for differences in price levels between countries provides a more accurate comparison of living standards. allows comparison of economic productivity and standards of living across different countries. … … … institutions economic historians such as robert fogel , david landes and douglas north have argued that the rich world is rich because, over the centuries, it has devised institutions that have enabled people to improve (1956). thermodynamics. courier corporation. @book{fermi1956thermodynamics, title={thermodynamics}, author={fermi, enrico}, year={1956}, publisher={courier corporation} } notes --- thermodynamics is mainly concerned with the transformation of heat into mechanical work and the opposite transformations of mechanical work into heat. note: heat is a form of energy; that can be changed into others forms of energy. note: in the past, heat was not thought as energy; but a fluid. note: the study of the steam engine. thermodynamic systems a thermodynamic state is a macroscopic, equilibrium-based specification of a system using a complete set of state variables. it encodes all the information needed to determine the system’s energy, entropy, and response to external constraints—while abstracting away the chaotic microscopic details. the state of a system in thermodynamics refers to a macroscopic description characterized by a set of thermodynamic variables. these variables—such as pressure, volume, temperature, and entropy—are not values of individual particles but represent ensemble averages over an enormous number of microscopic degrees of freedom. consequently, the thermodynamic state is an aggregated abstraction that smooths out molecular-level fluctuations. let’s say our thermodynamic system is a “system composed of a chemically homogeneous fluid”, we can measure the temperature $(t)$, volume $(v)$, pressure $(p)$. these variables obey the state equation $f (p, v , t) = 0$. a transformation is defined as a process in which a thermodynamic system undergoes a change of state. during such a transformation, the system may exchange energy with its surroundings in the form of heat or work, thereby affecting its environment . the second law of thermodynamics … the entropy … thermodynamic potentials … gaseous reactions … the thermodynamics of dilute solutions … the entropy constant … references - https://archive.org/details/thermodynamics0000ferm/mode/2up

(2014). systems performance: enterprise and the cloud. pearson education. @book{gregg2014systems, title={systems performance: enterprise and the cloud}, author={gregg, brendan}, year={2014}, publisher={pearson education} } notes --- systems performace system performace is the study of the entire sysetm (software stack + hardware stack) / anything in the data path. data path is the physical and logical component of a computer system responsible for executing instructions and performing data manipulation tasks. systems performance engineering is a challenging field for a number of reasons, includ- ing the fact that it is subjective, it is complex, and it often involves multiple issues. it is a capital mistake to theorize before one has data. insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts. sherlock holmes in “a scandal in bohemia” by sir arthur conan doyle the performance of the system under increasing load is its scalability. system performance monitoring records performance statistics over time (a time series), so that the past can be compared to the present and time-based usage pat-terns can be identified. this is useful for capacity planning, quantifying growth, and showing peak usage. historic values can also provide context for understand- ing the current value of performance metrics, by showing what the “normal” range and average have been in the past. activities 1. setting performance objectives and performance modeling 2. performance characterization of prototype software or hardware 3. performance analysis of development code, pre-integration 4. performing non-regression testing of software builds, pre- or post-release 5. benchmarking/benchmarketing for software releases 6. proof-of-concept testing in the target environment 7. configuration optimization for production deployment 8. monitoring of running production software 9. performance analysis of issues perspectives https://i.imgur.com/5f1qnjo.png analysis perspectives resource analysis resource analysis begins with amarlow, s., & jones, s. p. (1998). the new ghc/hugs runtime system. url http://research. microsoft. com/apps/pubs/default. aspx, 2. nalysis of the system resources: cpus, memory, disks, network interfaces, busses, and interconnects. some metrics: - iops - throughput - utilization - saturation workload analysis workload analysis examines the performce of the application. https://i.imgur.com/e82zam5.png workload analysis the targets for workload analysis are: - requests : the workload applied - latency : the response time of the application - completion : looking for errors @book{gregg2014systems, title={systems performance: enterprise and the cloud}, author={gregg, brendan}, year={2014}, publisher={pearson education} } analytical modeling analytical modeling of a system can be used for various purposes, in particular scalability analysis: studying how performance scales as load or resources scale. resources may be hardware, such as cpu cores, or software, such as processes or threads. https://i.imgur.com/yaispw8.png scalability … system models the system under test refers to the specific software, hardware, or combination thereof that is being evaluated, tested, or analyzed in a given context or experiment. https://i.imgur.com/o48xep1.png sut templates: - system under test (sut) - queueing modele systems layer tuning targets --- --- layer tuning targets application database queries performed database database table layout, indexes, buffering system calls memory-mapped or read/write, sync or async i/o flags file system record size, cache size, file system tunables storage raid level, number and type of disks, storage tunables marlow, s., & jones, s. p. (1998). the new ghc/hugs runtime system. url http://research. microsoft. com/apps/pubs/default. aspx, 2. metrics - response time : the time for an operation to complete. this includes any time spent waiting and time spent being serviced (service time), including the time to transfer the result. - iops : input/output operations per second is a measure of the rate of data transfer operations. for disk i/o, iops refers to reads and writes per second. - latency : latency is a measure of time an operation spends waiting to be serviced. in some contexts, it can refer to the entire time for an operation, equivalent to response time. see section 2.3, concepts, for examples. - throughput : the rate of work performed. especially in communications, the term is used to refer to the data rate (bytes per second or bits per second). in some contexts (e.g., databases), throughput can refer to the operation rate (operations per second or transactions per second). ut ilization : for resources that service requests, utilization is a measure of how busy a resource is, based on how much time in a given interval it was actively performing work. for resources that provide storage, utilization may refer to the capacity that is consumed (e.g., memory utilization). - saturation : the degree to which a resource has queued work it cannot service. - bottleneck : in system performance, a bottleneck is a resource that limits the performance of the system. identifying and removing systemic bottlenecks is a key activity of systems performance. - workload : the input to the system or the load applied is the workload. for a database, the workload consists of the database queries and commands sent by the clients. techniques - dynamic tracing - profiling methodologies @book{gregg2014systems, title={systems performance: enterprise and the cloud}, author={gregg, brendan}, year={2014}, publisher={pearson education} } analysis tools. methodology type --- --- streetlight anti-method observational analysis random change anti-method experimental analysis blame-someone-else anti-method hypothetical analysis ad hoc checklist method observational and experimental analysis problem statement information gathering scientific method observational analysis diagnosis cycle analysis life cycle tools method observational analysis use method observational analysis workload characterization observational analysis, capacity planning drill-down analysis observational analysis latency analysis observational analysis method r observational analysis event tracing observational analysis baseline statistics observational analysis performance monitoring observational analysis, capacity planning queueing theory statistical analysis, capacity planning static performance tuning observational analysis, capacity planning cache tuning observational analysis, tuning micro-benchmarking experimental analysis capacity planning capacity planning, tuning workload characterization workload characterization is a simple and effective method for identifying a class of issues: those due to the load applied. workloads can be characterized by answering the following questions: - who is causing the load? process id, user id, remote ip address? - why is the load being called? code path, stack trace? - what are the load characteristics? iops, throughput, direction (read/write), type? include variance (standard deviation) where appropriate. - how is the load changing over time? is there a daily pattern? … @book{gregg2014systems, title={systems performance: enterprise and the cloud}, author={gregg, brendan}, year={2014}, publisher={pearson education} }

documents.text: husserl, e. (1900–1901). logical investigations. walter de gruyter. @book{husserl1900logical, title = {logical investigations}, author = {husserl, edmund}, year = {1900--1901}, publisher = {walter de gruyter}, address = {berlin}, isbn = {9783111821801}, note = {originally published in german as "logische untersuchungen"} } notes --- originally published in two volumes (1900–1901), logical investigations ( logische untersuchungen ) is one of the foundational works of 20th-century philosophy and the text that inaugurates phenomenology as a rigorous philosophical method. phenomenology take a ratoinalist premise of attributing identity to the self phenomenology arises as the rationalist attempt to recover the self’s foundation — but it collides with the self’s mutability. phenomenology as a restauration of pure logic. the self thought history has been described as ‘permanent - static’ - a huge mistake. which objects are permanent - “abstract mental objects” - universals (categories) - concepts - etc. index guide how to study this book? which research problems? which technical terminology? which underlying meta-theory? which underlying methods? how to validate husserl results? research problems: - (psychologism) can logic be reduced to psychology, or does it possess an objective, normative validity independent of human thought? - intentionality how do thoughts refer to objects, and what is the structure of consciousness that allows for this “aboutness”? - essence of logic what is the essence of logic as a normative science, and how can its laws of validity be rigorously grounded? - self as subject how can the self be given as a stable subject of knowledge, capable of providing a coherent standpoint for experience? - universals how do universal concepts—such as species, numbers, or essences—exist, and how can they be apprehended in consciousness? - justification and evidence what justifies knowledge, and what makes it evident , rather than merely believed or assumed? - temporal constitution how does consciousness constitute the flow of time, integrating past, present, and future in experience? methods: - phenomenological reduction (epoché) : suspend assumptions about the world to focus on consciousness itself. - eidetic analysis : identify essential structures of experiences or concepts. - intentional analysis : examine how mental acts are directed toward objects. 📘 volume i — prolegomena to pure logic introduction - §1. the task of logic - §2. the psychological and the logical - §3. the relation between logic and psychology part one: theories of knowledge and logic chapter i. the psychological standpoint and the psychologistic prejudice chapter ii. empiricism, logicism, and psychologism chapter iii. the confusion of logic with psychology in empirical theories of knowledge chapter iv. the confusion of logic with psychology in pure logic part two: the idea of a pure logic chapter i. logic as a theoretical discipline chapter ii. the idea of pure logic as a formal theory of science chapter iii. pure logic as the foundation of all sciences chapter iv. the systematic unity of pure logic part three: the fundamental problems of pure logic chapter i. pure grammar and the logical forms of meaning chapter ii. the pure theory of manifolds chapter iii. the pure theory of inference and theory of knowledge chapter iv. the idea of a formal ontology conclusion - logic as a normative and theoretical science - the autonomy of pure logic - the delimitation of pure logic from psychology and from theory of knowledge 📗 volume ii — investigations in phenomenology and the theory of knowledge introduction - transition from formal logic to phenomenology - the concept of meaning and the task of descriptive analysis first investigation: expression and meaning - i. the distinction between expression and indication - ii. the meaning of expressions - iii. the ideal unity of meaning - iv. the problem of meaning and object second investigation: the ideal unity of the species and modern theories of abstraction - i. the difference between empirical and ideal objects - ii. the concept of species and essence - iii. critique of nominalism and conceptualism - iv. abstraction and intuition third investigation: on the theory of wholes and parts - i. the dependence and independence of parts - ii. the laws of part–whole relations - iii. the foundation of mereology - iv. categories of dependence and inseparability fourth investigation: the distinction between independent and dependent meanings - i. syntactic dependence of expressions - ii. formal grammar and logical syntax - iii. the structure of complex meanings fifth investigation: on intentional experiences and their “contents” - i. the concept of intentionality - ii. acts and contents - iii. the noetic–noematic correlation - iv. objectivity and consciousness sixth investigation: elements of a phenomenological elucidation of knowledge - i. presentation, intuition, and fulfillment - ii. evidence and truth - iii. the gradations of evidence - iv. the phenomenological reduction (in germinal form) qa - which are the limits of rationalism? - which is a mental object? what is the structure of the space of mental object? does a concept exist in reality? - what is essence? - what does ontic means? what the relation with ontology? - what is meant by the psychological basis of thinking? what is the psychological basis of logic? - what distinguishes subjectivity of knowledge from the objectivity of the objects of knowledge? - what is the form of knowledge? what is the difference between knowledge itself and the matter in which it is expressed? - what is the philosophical theory of pure mathematics ? a theory of mathematical concepts, methods, a theory of mathematical understanding. - are we rational? what rational means? - we improve and changed, if rationality means being right - then we are not rational. rationality is a property of the process of reason - or mental computation - not the result itself. references - 1 - 2 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/logical investigations (husserl) - https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/franz brentano - https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/carl stumpf - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/rationalism

(1865). history of materialism and criticism of its present importance. leipzig: verlag von duncker & humblot. @book{lange1865, author = {friedrich albert lange}, title = {history of materialism and criticism of its present importance}, publisher = {leipzig: verlag von duncker & humblot}, year = {1865}, address = {leipzig}, note = {original german edition; english translation by ernest c. thomas published 1877} } notes --- … index the early atomists, especially demokritos materialism is old as philosophy, but not older. how to fix the vulgar error of the senses? early formalization of logic. does logic help to explain? what’s the weakness of logic? what theory of matter does the atomist have? introduction of an effective concept of atom - and make that the substratum of all phenomena. out of nothing arises nothing; nothing that is can be destroyed. all change is only combination and separation of atoms. nothings happens by change, but everything thought a cause and of necessity. nothing exist but atoms and empty space; all else is only opinion. the atoms are infinite in number, and of endless variety of form. in the eternal fall through infinite space, the greater, which fall more quickly, strike against the lesser - and lateral movements and vortices - that thus arise are the commencement of the formation of worlds. innumerable worlds are formed and perish successively and simultaneously. the variety of all things is a consequence of the variety of their atoms is number, size, figure, and arrangement; there is no qualitative difference of atoms. they have not ‘internals conditions;’ and act on each other only by pressure or collision. the soul … the early atomists — mainly leucippus and democritus (5th century bce), and later epicurus and lucretius — indeed created a conceptual system to explain all of reality in terms of atoms (indivisible particles) and void (empty space). they introduced this idea not from observation but as an abstract explanatory principle — an attempt to reduce the complexity of the world to a few fundamental, intelligible elements. they then used that model to explain phenomena such as change, motion, perception, and even the soul, without invoking divine or teleological causes. for instance, they explained perception as the interaction of atomic “films” (eidola) with our sense organs, and change as the rearrangement of atoms. they didn’t have empirical methods in the modern sense — their reasoning was philosophical and speculative , driven by logical consistency and the desire for a naturalistic worldview . so, while they applied the atomic theory to phenomena, it was at the level of conceptual modeling , not experimentation. many forms of irrational or pre-scientific thinking indeed arise from anthropomorphism — the projection of human qualities (agency, purpose, intention, emotion) onto non-human entities or processes. examples include: - believing that natural events (storms, diseases, earthquakes) happen for a reason or to teach a lesson . - attributing intent to random or mechanical processes (“the universe wanted this to happen”). - treating abstractions as moral or personal agents (“justice will punish them,” “nature is angry”). cognitive science explains this as a byproduct of evolved social cognition — our brains are specialized to detect agents, intentions, and social patterns, even when none exist. this “hyperactive agency detection” helped our ancestors survive but can misfire in abstract reasoning. much irrational thinking stems from our tendency to anthropomorphize — to project human agency, purpose, and intention onto the impersonal or random — though other cognitive biases also play major roles. ontology: dimension category description --- --- (2019). the art of economic catch-up: barriers, detours and leapfrogging in innovation systems. cambridge university press. @book{lee2019art, title={the art of economic catch-up: barriers, detours and leapfrogging in innovation systems}, author={lee, keun}, year={2019}, publisher={cambridge university press} } notes --- the art of economic catch-up description of the process of catching up (development): its barriers, failures (lack of capacity), and some solutions (detours) / leap- frog / find a new path. the economic literature endeavors to find a universal factor for economic growth that will bind all countries, regardless of income level and structural differences. development generally refers to growth, progress, or advancement toward a goal or desired state. imitation → innovation to avoid the catch-up paradox (one cannot catch-up only by imitation). exploration on how firms and nations develop. this books begging with an exploration of the mechanisms of growth (rich, poor, develop) - some strategies (detours) to catch-up - some specific techniques to cultivate technological capabilities - how to promote big businesses - windows of opportunity (leap-frogging) to capture some emergent market. it’s a great book that try to explore ways in which late-commers can catch-up barriers : - intellectual property rights (ipr) protect advanced economies. failures (lack of capacity): - firm capability : hard to build innovation capabilities, - size - or not firms at all . failures : lack of world-class business in developing countries. what detours to take? - from imitative - innovation. - from short-cycle to long-cycle - more, less, and more gvc again specific advice : - enter a low-end segment free from competition from the advanced economies. - imitative innovation: under a loose ipr regime in the form of petit patents and trademarks instead of promoting and strengthening regular pattern rights. - gvc: increase integration, decrease integration, to later increase integration again. - use the global value chain to learn, then establish local value chains. - the establishment of local value chains is vital for competitiveness. - short cycle technology: specialise in short cycle technological sectors like (it) and only go long cycles like (pharmaceuticals) at later stages. - investing in education and research and development, - promoting industrial clusters, - and implementing policies that support innovation and entrepreneurship. leapfrog : take a technology - use it / explore it first; use that window of opportunity (when the advanced economies are using good enough technologies). find a new path : - find an unexplored new technology, - find a unsolves-problems for unexplored markets, - … economic well-being is achieved once a society improves its computational engine either by: - learning how to compute new products by learning how to compute products more efficiently. references - what is a terminal? - does every process have a terminal? - how many terminals are created by the os? tty1, … - what is the anatomy of a process address space? who determines that anatomy? index overview history and goals multics history. unix history. unix was written in a high level language / c. unix distribution: … freebsd organization model: … bsd: berkeley software distribution. computer systems research group (csrg): … portable operating system interface ( posix) - 1988. bsd: unix + utilities → core contributions (socket api, tcp/ip stack, ffs, virtual memory, job control, signals, …) → increasingly independent bsd code → at&t/usl legal dispute → settlement → 4.4bsd-lite (at&t code removed) → bsd-derived operating systems (freebsd, netbsd, openbsd, dragonfly bsd). berkeley software distribution (bsd) originated at the university of california, berkeley, as a set of enhancements to the at&t unix operating system. the first bsd release appeared in 1977 (1bsd) , primarily distributing additional software developed at berkeley, including the ex editor and pascal tools. during the late 1970s and early 1980s, bsd evolved from a collection of unix additions into a substantial operating-system distribution. 4.1bsd (1981) and subsequent releases introduced major improvements in performance, virtual memory, networking, and system utilities. a major milestone was 4.2bsd (1983) , which incorporated tcp/ip networking , the berkeley sockets api, and the fast file system (ffs). these mechanisms became foundational to internet-connected unix systems and were subsequently adopted widely. with 4.3bsd (1986) and later releases, berkeley continued improving networking, kernel performance, and system facilities. the bsd unix source code also became increasingly important as a basis for other unix systems. in the early 1990s, berkeley separated much of its independently developed code from at&t's proprietary unix code. the 4.4bsd-lite releases provided a largely freely redistributable bsd system and became the direct ancestor of modern bsd operating systems such as freebsd, netbsd, and openbsd . time line of bd contribution set unix extensions → virtual memory → bsd utilities → fast file system (ffs) → tcp/ip stack → berkeley sockets api → network programming model → performance & kernel improvements → open bsd source → bsd as an independent unix system bsd: core people and institutions - bill joy — co-founder of bsd; central figure in early berkeley unix, ex/vi , networking, and the bsd distribution. - chuck haley — worked with joy on the early berkeley unix environment and helped develop ex . - ken thompson — co-creator of unix; important because bsd originated as modifications and extensions to at&t unix. - dennis ritchie — co-creator of unix and c; c was fundamental to bsd's implementation. - kirk mckusick — major bsd developer; central to the fast file system (ffs) and later bsd development. - marshall kirk mckusick — same person; often cited as kirk mckusick . - sam leffler — major contributor to 4.2bsd/4.3bsd , particularly networking and system development. - mike karels — important bsd kernel and networking developer; later involved in the bsd legal and organizational transition. - eric allman — developed sendmail , one of the major pieces of software distributed with bsd. - keith bostic — key figure in removing at&t-derived code and producing 4.4bsd-lite . - chris torek — important contributor to the c/compiler and bsd development ecosystem. - theo de raadt — founder of openbsd . - jordan hubbard — co-founder and early leader of freebsd . - lynne jolitz & william jolitz — produced 386bsd , an important ancestor of freebsd, netbsd, and openbsd. - matthew dillon — founder of dragonfly bsd . - bell labs / at&t — creator and original owner of unix. - university of california, berkeley (ucb) — home of the bsd project. - computer systems research group (csrg), uc berkeley — the primary institutional group behind bsd development. - darpa — major sponsor of berkeley networking research, especially the tcp/ip work. - usl (unix system laboratories) — at&t subsidiary that pursued the legal case against bsd. - berkeley software design, inc. (bsdi) — commercial company founded around bsd technology and involved in the unix/bsd legal dispute. the freebsd development model - core developer: a selected group of people elected every two years by the committers. gatekeepers of the source code. - control model of code merging into the main developmetn line: … - screenign process: - code review & approval mechanism: … - organization: similar to csrg: code, documentation, bug report database, mailing list, administrative data, it’s maintain publicly. - software development process automation - specially of repetitive operations. - https://www.freebsd.org/administration/ design overview of freebsd the freebsd kernel provides process, filesystem, communication, and a system startup. kernel: $h$ → $h {vm}$ is the core component of an operating system that abstracts the physical hardware $h$ into a virtualized, abstract hardware model ($h {vm}$). it provides user processes with a secure and consistent interface to interact with system resources, translating high-level operations into hardware-specific instructions. - how to model the hardware? - what is hardware ? - what is the structure of a modern computer system ? - which is the hardware type space ? bus, … - which are the types of mechanisms by which hardware entities interact with other hardware in the computer? and how, through the cpu, can one communicate with them? which are the connectivity mechanism hierarchy (up - directly interact with the cpu), lower (does not)? - how is hardware detected and configured by the system? - how to formulate the $h {vm}$? how does it abstracts hardware? - how is $h {vm}$ implemented? kernel implementation abstractions (implementation): … kernel services (interface / specification): … the machine-dependent aspects of the kernel are isolated from the mainstream code. the kernel operate in a different address space that is inaccessible to user processes. free bsd kernel services: - basic kernel facilities: timer and system-clock handling, descriptor management, and process management, - memory-management support: paging and swapping, - generic system interfaces: the i/o, control, and multiplexing operations performed on descriptors, - the filesystem: files, directories, pathname translation implementation abstractions: - basic: timer and system clock-handling, descriptor management, and process management, - memory-management support: paging and swapping, - generic system interfaces, i/o, control, and multiplexing operations performed on descriptors, - the filesystem: files, directories, pathname translation, file locking, and i/o buffer management - terminal-handling support: the pseudo-terminal interface and terminal line disciplines - interprocess-communication facilities: sockets - support for network communication: communication protocols and generic work facilities, such as routing machine dependent software: - low-level system-startup actions, - trap and fault-handling - low-level manipulation of the run-time context of a process - configuration and inititialization of hardware devices - run-time support for i/o devices system call: - service interface of the kernel. - a system call usually is implemented as hardware trap that changes the cpu’s execution mode and the current address-space mapping. process management: - a thread or task of execution if called a process. - processes are scheduled for execution according to a process priority parameter. - real-time process have the highest priority and did not need to share the underlying resources. - process are organized in process groups. - process groups : are used to control access to terminals an to provide a means of distributing signals to collection of related process. signals: - the system defines a set of signal that may be delivered to a process. a signal like many other concepts can be define networking - what is the minimum trasmision unit of x technolgy? memory management : - each process has it’s own private address space. the address space is initially divided into three logical segments: text, data, and stack. the text segment is read-only and contains the machine instructions of a program. - nmap: allow a process to extend it’s address space using a an external file. kernel memory management : - the kernel stack is limited; - most kernel allocation are dynamic (not stack or what?) i/0 system: - the basic model of the unix i/o system is a sequence of bytes that can be accessed either randomly or sequentially. - i/o stream: an stream of bytes. descriptors and i/o: - unix processes use descriptors to reference i/o streams. descriptors are small unsigned integers obtained from the open and socket system calls. - descriptors can denote file, pipe, fifo and socket . descriptor management: - standard descriptors in proccesses? input, output; error. - descriptor remmaping: i/o redirection - pipeline: a series of proceses connected by pipes. devices: - hardware devices have filenames and many be accessed by the user via the same system calls used for regular files. - device special file / special file. - network devices uses syscalls; and not files; because interaction between two end-points it’s hard to model as a filed. socket: - socket ipc: a communication endpoint; it denoted by a file descriptor. scatter/gather i/o: - multiple buffer - single read. kernel services saying that the kernel is a service provider to userlang - to me is a wrong formulation. the kernel - fundamental provides a abstract interface to the underlying hardware - that is it exposed the capabilities of the hardware though a interaction interface. i need to reason very deeply - about the concept of technical service, and if this concept - match the piece of reality - being abstracted via the concept. interaction interface: - syscalls ( ioctl, mmap ), - /proc - /sys - ptty - device files - signals - shared memory - ipc interfaces - sockets - virtual filesystems … - system process - kernel process - execution abstractions - process - kernel process - process group - permanent kernel proceses - what can trigger the executing of the kernel code? hardware interrupt, hardware trap, software-initiated trap (which is also hardware 😎). - 👁️ what is the difference between a trap and a interrupt? https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3149175/what-is-the-difference-between-trap-and-interrupt - they are both events, the difference comes from role, triggering mechanism, etc. - … cpu execution │ ▼ event / \ synchronous asynchronous (exception) (interrupt) │ │ ▼ ▼ handler handler - run time organization of the kernel: top half, button half. - entry to the kernel: when we switch from user process - the kernel must save the current state? - how does this works? - what happens with new inputs? networking, and other kinds of devices. - how the returning to the process happens? while process p is suspended in kernel context, how are concurrent external events handled, and under what semantics are they eventually delivered to p, coalesced, or discarded? process p ──► kernel ───────────────► resume p │ │ p's context saved │ ├───────┐ │ │ concurrent event │ ▼ │ [mouse / i/o / network] │ │ │ ▼ │ kernel handling │ │ │ ▼ └────► ? │ queued / coalesced / dropped │ ▼ delivered to p? - is a system call a trap ? - what is a page ? - which security capabilities does freebsd offer, and how are they implemented ? - how to control the underlying resources? assigments, … - how the accoutnign works? how the os keeps tracks of the resources being consume? processes process management memory management i/o system i/o system overview device local filesystems the network filesystem terminal handling interprocess communication interprocess communication network communication network protocols system operation startup and shutdown qa how is the io bus implemented? how to list the bus recognize by the os (linux/ubuntu) ? … which technique is behind the design of the memory paging mechanism? model-mediated abstraction technique : complex system → simplified model → human operates on the model → translation layer → real system. and there are several distinct products of the technique: 1. representation abstraction — hide implementation details. 2. interface abstraction — expose a smaller interaction surface. 3. execution abstraction — make one computational system appear as another. 4. resource abstraction — turn physical resources into logical resources. 5. isolation abstraction — make shared resources appear private. 6. semantic abstraction — represent low-level operations using higher-level concepts. 7. translation mechanism — maintain correspondence between model and reality. 8. composition mechanism — allow models to be combined into larger models. which are the origins of the term ‘unix’? the term unix came from unics , a pun on multics . - multics = multiplexed information and computing service - unics = originally uniplexed information and computing service - it was later spelled unix . which are the set of concepts that renders the freebsd interaction surface intelligible? commands, utilities, system calls, files, processes, signals, pipes, sockets, devices, filesystems, users, groups, permissions, shells, daemons, configuration mechanisms, apis, and abis. what is the quality of the concepts that emerge from the interface? is there overlap between them? the concepts are primarily abstractions of resources, operations, actors, and interaction mechanisms. they exhibit substantial conceptual coherence and composability, but also intentional overlap: the same underlying resource may be exposed through multiple interfaces. the key question is whether these overlaps preserve distinct and predictable semantics or introduce conceptual redundancy and ambiguity. which are the set of concepts that renders the freebsd implementation intelligible? kernels, subsystems, modules, kernel objects, data structures, system-call implementations, processes and threads, schedulers, virtual memory, vfs, filesystems, device drivers, networking, ipc, synchronization mechanisms, interrupt and trap handling, resource management, protection mechanisms, abi compatibility layers, and hardware-abstraction mechanisms. what is the quality of the concepts that emerge from the implementation? is there overlap between them? the implementation concepts are more concrete and mechanism-oriented. they form a layered and highly interconnected conceptual structure, with significant overlap at subsystem boundaries. this overlap is generally functional rather than redundant: multiple mechanisms may participate in realizing a single abstraction, while a single implementation mechanism may support several abstractions. references -
