(1848). principles of political economy with some of their applications to social philosophy. john w. parker. @book{mill1848principles, author = {mill, john stuart}, title = {principles of political economy with some of their applications to social philosophy}, year = {1848}, publisher = {john w. parker}, address = {london} } notes --- economic phenomena : money supply and prices. in his notes on prosperity , mill does not include metatechnical factors or changes in the technical corpus. while he mentions innovation in the note on labor as indirect, he does not treat it as an integral part of the description of economic reality. note: mills uses technique ( technology, the arts of production) not as first class citizen of it’s theory - but a second class explanatory mechanism - that he brings from time to time. index sketch on the history of political economy mill hace un inventario de los escritos sobre la historia de la policia economica en la lengua inglesa. blanqui’s “historie de l’economie polique en europe”, villenueve-bargrmont - “historie de l’economie politique”, … recognotino of the phenomnea to study & evolution of ideas - is basically what we want of a history of political economy . aristotle xenophon; plato, economic thinking in roman times. what is the history of the term economy ? middle wages economic thought. mill in the book uses the idea that ‘spain’ (not understanding the empire - or the complex system of governance of the monarchy) - stablish a mercantile system, trying to keep the gold to himself (not knowing that the monary only control the taxes on gold, silver, etc - and that a great part of precius metals used to mind coins - was used for the commerce with asia. ). etc. “look for more data on this.”. mill charcterization of mercatalism - thoery and praxis it’s problematic - seems there was not a standard praxis nor books - yes the remarks of mill applys (acculation, all exports non imports), etc - but some mercantilist were all about value added, and technology etc. so this is a partial characterization of the distribution of ‘informally - ill identified group’. mill trace the protection of home industry, and the balance of trade - history of navigation laws, … colbert - loius xiv. mill ways that colbert was almost resonsable of starving rural areas - becuase it’s practices bring tarrifs wars - that affected agriculture. the psysiocrats . francois quesnay. → laissez faire, laissez passer . adam smith contribution according to mill - labor was basis of production, not agriculture. skill of the labor . price vs value → … fixed vs circulating capital? capital vs money? ideas of population and economy. law of rent. law of diminishing return from land. ricardo comparative cost . patent abolition ideas history. historical method used in germany. economic laws can only be study by induction - books for consulation preliminary remarks production i. of the prerequisites of production (→ pg 52) summary: …. notes: - the requisites of production are two: labor , appropriate natural objects and capital. (what is appropriate natural objects? are machines this? or only nature inputs?) - when a laborer devotes himself to a type of activity whose outputs cannot, via nutritional provision, sustain his biological functions, capital enters the scene. (re-writing) - labor is fundamentally either bodily or mental. (note: mental labor is also physical; the distinction concerns whether the primary output of labor consists in the use of bodily actuators to produce direct physical changes in the world.) - appropriate natural objects with this mill basically means the biological natural elements which their outputs either directly or indirectly can serve as products usable by humans - fruits, honey, land, coal, etc. - natural objects derive economic value from scarcity; in the absence of limitation, market value collapses. - mill proposes a categorization of labor as direct product (baker, miner) and indirect or enabler (complementary) of production (transportation, inventor). - labor is cumulative : labor embodied (reified) in a product can later function as a cooperative and facilitating input for new labor directed toward new ends. ( labor aggregation ). - … - … ii. of unproductive labor how does labor impact wealth—or the capacity to satisfy the needs and desires of everyone? - labor is the main input for production - but it can be used for other non ‘production’ related activities. (what does he means by non production here?) - productive labor means labor productive of wealth. - unproductive labor – labor that does not generate a net increase in social production. in other words, it is labor employed without producing more than it consumes. for example: - productive case: labor invested in saving the life of a worker—this preserves human capital that can continue contributing to production. - unproductive case: labor spent preserving obsolete machinery (e.g., an old mill no longer in use), which does not yield a net gain in production. - note: social reality is complex . applying a strict “productive vs. unproductive” distinction can generate feedback effects that destabilize society, because not all labor outcomes are easily reducible to net production. some activities may appear unproductive but carry indirect or long-term societal benefits. - productive labor can produce waste - be render unproductive - if the results are not consume. iii. of capital - what does mill means by ‘of capital’? - labor and natural objects are the fundamental elements of production, but without a third element— capital, the results of past production —industry can only remain in simple forms. (mill did not understand the fundamental source of wealth - latent techniques or meta-techniques). - saved wealth devoted to production. - note: capital is an abstract concept - almost an epitemological element that can denote elements of multiple form - united by a their functional role. - capital is an ontic - epistemic element (things that are not capital today - can become capital tomorrow). - what distinguishes wealth, money, and capital? wealth (value goods) is {money, capital}, money = {capital + non capital}. - money is only a technology to exchange (transfer) wealth. - … iv. fundamentals propositions respecting capital - industry is limited by capital → production is limited by capital. (actually this is wrong - industry is limited also - by technical knowledge - in this is one of the most fundamental limitations, among probably other things ). - increase of capital → can enable more industry → that used more labor. (not necessarily with automation). - capital it’s the result of saving. - things that are produced are intended for consumption (as final or intermediate). - the process of capital accumulation → production → saving → production → more saving → each saving increase the amount of capital . (actually this is false - this is a local observation - modulared by the technical set - and latent techniques (meta techniques)). - the structural constraint (technical set) - the dynamic constraint (research capacity = latent techniques → technogenesis - innovation capacity) - …. v. on circulating and fixed capital what is the taxonomy of capital? which are the dimensions of that taxonomy? which are the possibles taxonomy, that is taxonomy space? which are the dimesions set to specify such taxonomy? - capital that performs the entirety of its productive function within a single act of use is termed circulating capital . - capital whose productive function is not exhausted in a single use, but persists through repeated production processes, is termed fixed capital . - note: this chapter is basically about the definition and operationalization of the definition - nothing more. vi. of causes affecting the efficiency of production - the most evident (first) cause of superior productiveness is what are called natural advantages. fertility of soil is one of them. - some crazy things (like in hot climates people required less food intake) ??? what backs this up mr. mill? - the second cause of great productiveness is the energy of labor . - the third cause of great productiveness is the skill and knowledge. - the productivity of labor is also impact by the technical objects complements. - division of labor (impact on productivity) - the division of labor is impacted by the nature of the activity - can it be decomposed into a set of tasks (can those tasks be parallelize, etc.) - this requires scale of the tasks (that is basically enterprise scale). - other secondaries: - security to the members of the society. - co-operation - or the combined action of members. - how were large-scale firms brought into existence through the joint-stock mechanism? - on the effect on the numbers of firms on competition? does a market with two firms is better off than a market with one firm? vii. on the laws of increase labor - basically on increase population. viii. of the law of the increase of capital what determine capital formation ? note: capital accumulation depends on the dynamics of technical knowledge. a stagnant technical space leads to stagnant capital formation. (my take) - since all capital is in the product of savings, so from this we saving depends on the size of the fund from which it’s save, and the rate of saving. - stationary state - of capital - when not more capital can be added, because of stagnation in the product space (either more products or techniques that can make new products possible) - capital is the product of pass labor (actually only r&d labor) . ix. of the law of increase of production from land - land supply is fixed. - the law of diminishing returns is the physical fact upon which the economic doctrine of rent is based. ?? - mill’s answer is essentially technique (tools, infrastructure, etc.): intelligence dominates nature; multiple intelligences working synergistically surpass a single intelligence. x. consequences of documents.text: mitchell, m. (2009). complexity: a guided tour. oxford university press. notes --- many phenomena have stymied the reductionist program: the seemingly irreducible unpredictability of weather and climate, the adaptability of living systems, the complexity of societies, and more. these persistent challenges lend weight to the anti-reductionist catchphrase, ‘the whole is more than the sum of its parts,’ which gains significance from these failures. reductionism: rooted in rené descartes' method of analysis, this approach involves breaking down complex problems into smaller, more manageable components to facilitate systematic understanding and resolution. frameworks to model complex systems: - cybernetics : study of regulatory systems (feedback, control). - synergetics : interdisciplinary study of spontaneous order in complex systems. - systems science : holistic analysis of systems across domains. - complex systems science : emergence, nonlinearity, and adaptation in networks. index qa: - can simple rules generate complex and adaptive behavior in systems? background and history what is complexity? ideas thus made up of several simple ones put together, i call complex; such as are beauty, gratitude, a man, an army, the universe. - john locke, an essay concerning human understanding. how do entities—such as humans and ants—cooperate to build larger structures that enhance their overall probability of survival? how do cells organize themselves to form complex organs like the eye or the brain? how does intelligence emerge from non-intelligent matter? complex system: a system in which large networks of component with no central control and simple rules of operation give rise to complex collective behavior, sophisticated information processing, and adaptation via learning or evolution. complex system theory refers in our framework to systems consisting of a large network of interconnected components (nodes) without central control, where simple rules of operation lead to complex collective behaviors, advanced information processing, and adaptation through learning or evolution . emergent behavior : when interactions among a system's parts give rise to complex behaviors that are difficult to predict or derive from the behavior of the individual components. self-organizing : systems in which organized behavior emerges spontaneously without the need for central control. how can complexity be measured? as of today, there is no universally satisfactory definition for this question; many definitions and theories exist. case studies: - insect colonies (individual simplicity → collective sophistication ) : an individual ant is relatively simple, responding to chemical signals from nearby ants and driven by basic survival instincts . however, when ants work together as a group , they form a colony capable of achieving complex tasks far beyond the abilities of any single ant. these colonies can build intricate structures and demonstrate modular organization, accomplishing goals that no single ant could achieve alone. - the brain ( neurons → intelligence ): the brain is composed of various types of cells , but neuroscientists believe that neurons are the key ingredient from which thought, perception, and other large scale activities arise. - the immune system: (cell → human defense system): a collection of cells distributed across the body; without a central coordination mechanism. - [ note this is really an out of equilibrium system ] economies (actor - action → self organization of economic processes): an economy is a system in which a set of actors (e.g., producers, consumers, and intermediaries), through primarily local interactions—such as buying, selling, and bargaining—collectively and often unintentionally give rise to global patterns of production and distribution of goods and services. this emergent behavior reflects the self-organizing nature of economic processes, where no central authority necessarily directs all activity, yet coherent outcomes such as supply chains, pricing, and allocation arise. list of common denominators of complex systems: - emergent collective behavior : a system composed of individual components, each following simple rules, produces complex group dynamics without centralized control . - signaling & information processing : components generate, transmit, and interpret signals to coordinate with one another. - adaptation : the system dynamically adjusts its behavior in response to feedback, optimizing for survival, efficiency, or other key metrics. dynamics, chaos, and prediction … information … computation … evolution … genetics, simplified … defining and measuring complexity … life and evolution in computer … self-reproducing computer programs genetic algorithms computation writ large … cellular automata, life, and the universe computing with particles information processing in living systems how to make analogies (if you are a computer) prospects of computer modelling network thinking the science of networks applying network science to real-world networks the mystery of scaling evolution, complexified conclusion the past and future of the sciences of complexity references - https://www.complexityexplorer.org/courses/144-introduction-to-complexity-2022 - complexity course - hume, d. ones have to complement it with other materials. relativistic brain theory (rbt) is a new conceptual and physiological model that tries to explain (ground) how huge networks of interconected brain cells - known as neuron - are capable of both generating complex brain functions, ranging from mundane pain, to the sense of self and even consciousness, and, in striking contrast, diverge into pathological mental states, as the result of multitude of neurological or phychiatric disorders that can devastate one’s existence by altering the way our brains build perception of ourselves and the world around us. in this works (appendix 1) there is a detail set of experiments in order to test the theory. this work challenges a competing theory—the computationalist hypothesis—which posits that the brain functions like a digital computer. the book propose that the central nervous system generate, combine and store information about itself, the body and the external world through the recurrent dynamic interplay of a hybrid digital-analog computational engine . this computational engine works as follows: the electrical firing produced by widely distributed networks of neurons flows thought a large variety oi ‘biological coils’, formed by the nerve bundles of the brain’s white matter core, continously generating variable and complex electromagnetic fields (nemfs). rbt predicts that the manifold created by the continuos interferences of these nemfs works as a ‘biological analog computer’, the neuronal space-time continuum, from which a “mental space” emerges to underlie most of the brain’s higher order functions . this nemfs are not tractable or computable ??? references - (2021). crafting interpreters. genever benning. @book{nystrom2021crafting, title={crafting interpreters}, author={nystrom, robert}, year={2021}, publisher={genever benning} } notes --- … index introduction a programming language is a formally defined system of symbolic rules and syntactic constructs equipped with a semantics that maps well-formed expressions to computational behaviors or abstract machine transitions, enabling the precise specification, manipulation, and execution of algorithms and data structures. the mechanism by which we encode and express the rules that drive (underlies) a given computation. note: the pedagogy involves teaching language system concepts while developing two systems: an interpreter and a bytecode virtual machine. image.png a map of the territory “you must have a map, no matter how rough. otherwise you wander all over the place. in the lord of the rings i never made anyone go farther than he could on a given day.” - j. r. r. tolkien though a map simplifies and omits, it enables effective orientation within complex terrain. a map of the language system mountain. a map of the language system mountain. image.png the parts of a language: - scanning or lexing : a scanner (or lexer ) takes in the linear stream of characters and chunks them together into a series of something more akin to “words”. in programming languages, each of these words is called a token . some tokens are single characters, like ( and , . others may be several characters long, like numbers ( 123 ), string literals ( "hi!" ), and identifiers ( min ). - parsing (uncover the grammatical structure underlying a sentence) : a parser takes the flat sequence of tokens and builds a tree structure that mirrors the nested nature of the grammar. these trees have a couple of different names— parse tree or abstract syntax tree —depending on how close to the bare syntactic structure of the source language they are. in practice, language hackers usually call them syntax trees , asts , or often just trees . - static analysis : - binding or resolution : for each identifier , we find out where that name is defined and wire the two together. this is where scope comes into play—the region of source code where a certain name can be used to refer to a certain declaration. - type analysis : type checking, … - data models used for static analysis : … - control flow models - data flow models - abstract memory models - type and effect systems - program dependency graphs (pdg) - symbolic models - semantic and logical models - symbol table - program representation : - ir (intermediate representation) - … - optimization: once we understand what the user’s program means, we are free to swap it out with a different program that has the same semantics but implements them more efficiently—we can optimize it. - constant folding - … - code generation : we have applied all the optimizations we can think of to the user’s program. the last step is converting it to a form the machine can actually run. in other words, generating code (or code gen ), where “code” here usually refers to the kind of primitive assembly-like instructions a cpu runs and not the kind of “source code” a human might want to read. - virtual machine : a bytecode virtual machine (bvm) is an abstract computing architecture that executes programs represented in bytecode —a compact, intermediate, platform-independent binary format. the bvm emulates a cpu and runtime environment in software, interpreting or just-in-time compiling the bytecode into native machine instructions at runtime. - runtime: the collection of services, mechanisms, and infrastructure provided by the execution environment that supports and manages the behavior of a program while it runs. - taxonomy of language systems: - single pass compiler, - tree-walk interpreters, - transpiler, - just-in-time compilation - compiling is an implementation technique that involves translating a source language to some other—usually lower-level—form. when you generate bytecode or machine code, you are compiling. when you transpile to another high-level language, you are compiling, too. - (2017). the practice of industrial policy. oxford university press. @book{page2017-hx, title = "the practice of industrial policy", editor = "page, john and tarp, finn", abstract = "abstract much of the information relevant to policy formulation for industrial development is held by the private sector, not by public officials. there is, therefore, fairly broad agreement in the development literature that some form of structured engagement---often referred to as close or strategic coordination---between the public and private sectors is needed, to assist in the design of appropriate policies and provide feedback on their implementation. there is less agreement on how that engagement should be structured, how its objectives be defined, and how success be measured. in fact, the academic literature provides little practical guidance on how governments interested in developing such a framework should go about doing it. the burden of this lack of guidance falls most heavily on africa, where---despite twenty years of growth---lack of structural transformation has slowed job creation and the pace of poverty reduction. in 2014, the korea international cooperation agency (koica) and united nations university world institute for development economics research (unu-wider) launched a joint research project: the practice of industrial policy. the aim is to help african policy makers develop better coordination between public and private sectors in order to identify the constraints to faster structural transformation and design, implement, and monitor policies to remove them. this book, written by national researchers and international experts, presents the results of that research by combining a set of analytical framing' essays on close coordination with case studies of successful and unsuccessful efforts at close coordination in africa and in comparator countries.", publisher = "oxford university press", series = "wider studies in development - what does negative numbers represent? - which are the properties of any mathematical system ? which are the properties of any mathematical system ?%20pr%2010e598edb79081caa556eb36b7b333bd.md) - what is a deep insight behind the commutation property? https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3247011/why-is-multiplication-a-commutative-operation 📘 breviarium a comprehensive exploration of the topic. nucleus (🧬) → deepest essence (what is the deepest essence?) telos (🎯) → intent (what is it for? toward what end is it directed?) techne (🛠️) → function / used (by what craft or process is it made to work?) - decomposition - compensation - distribution - comutation - lattice multiplication - operator algorithms - proporsional reasoning - numeric comparison - lattice multiplication idoneitas (📏) → suitability (how well is it fitted for its purpose?) limites (🚧) → limits (what are its boundaries? what constraints define its operation?) contextus (🌐) → context (what is the historical, cultural, or situational context in which this study occurs?) properties of arithmetic … exponents … number theory … fractions … equations and inequalities … decimals … ratios, conversions, and rates … percents … square roots … angles … perimeter and area … right triangles and quadrilaterals … data and statistics … counting … problem-solving strategies … which are the properties of any mathematical system ? here’s a structured table of metaproperties that can be used to analyze any mathematical system (e.g., arithmetic, set theory, logic). these properties describe the system’s behavior, limitations, and relationships to other systems: property definition examples --- --- --- consistency the system cannot derive both a statement and its negation. peano arithmetic (pa) is consistent if it doesn’t prove $1 = 0$. completeness every true statement in the system is provable. presburger arithmetic (additive arithmetic) is complete. soundness only true statements are provable. first-order logic is sound: if $\vdash \phi$, then $\models \phi$. decidability an algorithm exists to determine if any statement is provable. euclidean geometry is decidable (tarski, 1951). categoricity all models of the system are isomorphic (structurally identical). second-order peano axioms are categorical (unique model: $\mathbb{n}$. expressiveness the system can formalize certain classes of statements. zfc set theory can express almost all modern mathematics. independence a statement is independent if it can’t be proved or disproved in the system. continuum hypothesis (ch) is independent of zfc. finite axiomatizability the system can be defined with finitely many axioms. robinson arithmetic (q) is finitely axiomatizable; zfc is not. non-contradiction the system obeys the law of non-contradiction $\neg (p \land \neg p)$. classical logic satisfies this; paraconsistent logics do not. computational power the system’s ability to encode computation (e.g., turing-complete). lambda calculus, pa, and zfc are turing-complete. examples across systems system consistent? complete? decidable? categorical? --- --- --- --- --- propositional logic yes yes yes no (multiple models) presburger arithmetic yes yes yes no (non-standard models) peano arithmetic (pa) presumed no (gödel) no no zfc set theory presumed no no no euclidean geometry yes yes yes yes (second-order) references - https://artofproblemsolving.com/ebooks/prealgebra-ebook/c0toc - https://archive.org/details/progressivecomme00good/page/56/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/bwb ks-110-546/page/n15/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/treatiseon00west00smituoft/page/16/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/intellectualarit00rayj/page/n3/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/anelementaryari01wentgoog/page/n4/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/cu31924015973906/page/n11/mode/2up - https://archive.org/details/cu31924015973906/page/n11/mode/2up - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/presburger arithmetic - https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/christoph.haase/home/publication/haa-18/haa-18.pdf - https://www21.in.tum.de/teaching/sar/ss20/9.pdf - the computational complexity of presburger arithmetic https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6j9051vs

the natural continuation and completion of kant’s, as he based his own system on the ideality of space and time and on kant’s concept of the thing-in-itself, as expounded in the critique of pure reason . in his essay on the fourfold root of the principle of sufficient reason , schopenhauer explores the intellectual nature of perception, showing that from the limited data supplied by our senses, our cognitive faculty immediately and automatically constructs a detailed mental picture of the external world. this mental picture is a “re-presentation” of sensory data—a vorstellung of the intellect—fundamentally different from a mere figment of the imagination. principle of sufficient reason: for everything that exists, there is a reason why it is so and not otherwise. schopenhauer wanted to express the profound idea behind philosophy in a single thought, but he was unable to do so and therefore had to write a book - the masterpiece of - << die welt als wille und vorstellung - the thought is deeply related with metaphysics, ethics and aesthetics. a system of thought must always have an architectonic connection of coherence, - that is, when one part always connects another. - like a well connected liked a poset or a spanning tree. reading notes world as will + representation . - will = metaphysical ground of being (noumenal aspect) - representation = phenomenal manifestation (cognitive or perceptual aspect) reality under schopenhauer is a dynamic web of relations, constantly in flux, driven by a single, blind, and striving will—the fundamental force underlying all existence. atomistic notions of independent entities fail to capture this deeper reality; individual objects are merely transient appearances of the will’s continuous, flowing unity. why not interpret the concept of will as - energy and as a force? what is the different between a force - and energy? what is the hierarchy of representation? perception → …. in the history of philosophy schopenhauer’s name will always be associated with a correct distinction between knowledge of perception and abstract knowledge - with a proper analysis of consciousness, of the so-called psyche - into will and intellect, with the correct interpretation and utilization of the platonic ideas, and finally with a true insight into the real nature of christianity from both the religious and philosophical points of view. quam multa fieri non posse, priusquam sint facta, judicantur! → how many things are thought impossible until they have been accomplished! - plinio el viejo. schopenhauer’s denunciation of charlatans and sophistical masqueraders as philosophers. schopenhauer called hegel caliban and other insults. the title the world as will and representation is deeply indicative: it does not claim that the world is representation, but rather that it presents itself under two inseparable aspects— as representation , the world as it appears to the subject, and as will , the inner, striving essence that underlies all appearances. the idea of will means that beneath all appearances — which are merely representations, or interpretations of the outer world — there lies a single, inner reality : a blind, striving force that underlies and manifests itself in every phenomenon. the idea of will not about appearances - but thought appearances the deepest aspects of reality - and the phenomena it generates. ontological level note: what lives in reality; can live in the above layers also. note: what live in let’s say representation does not have to lived in quantity, universal, particular, relation, is a (type relation), category, property, modality, … note: one can’t confuse the notion of the grammar of representation with the grammar of reality. the grammar of representation can called also the “grammar of thought“. note: a grammar of representation is the grammar of reality plus the mechanisms to represent representations. in a deeper sense, the grammar of reality is itself a representation of representations, but it is independent of the observer — these are the representations of the most “objective” objects. grammar of reality aka. the defines the word welt = world as representation of reality . this is a definition - not an statement - we can discuss thought is this conception of the world the right one - should we have a word that denote’s the representation of reality, etc. is this a valid way to proced - does this definition has any value? - what does this definition tries to capture? - what implications for reality does this definition has? - schopenhauer; never state that the world = representation; just as representation - one aspect for sure is representation. this is an epistemological world (internal) - and the external world (reality.) - … wille: vorstellungen : … form = essence, structure, or principle that defines what a thing is. reading advice read schopenhauer’s work slowly and patiently, preferably twice. remember that the book is structured as a partially ordered set (poset), so it unfolds organically; this is why reading it in order is essential. read on the fourfold root of the principle of sufficient reason: a philosophical essay. read the introduction before the book. read kant. → there is an appendix that can help acquire the necessary knowledge of kant’s philosophy to prepare for this book. the world as representation the world is my representation . this is a valid statement for all living beings - but only humans can reflect on it. the ‘representation’ of ‘representation’ is the most general form - that exists. representation as the most fundamental form - representation - <<object - subject ; the world is representation. every other form (category) can be castes in terms of representation - causality, time, being, etc. we act based on our representation of the world , but we must recognize—and accept—that our representations are never perfect. sometimes they are significantly flawed or even arbitrary. this realization is complex and carries profound psychological implications. all representations are expressions of the underlying will; ultimately, reality in itself is nothing but will. - the will underlies everything. that which knows all things and is known by none is the subjec t. - representation. representation: - object: whose forms are space and time - structure and dynamics. - subject: ??? - principle of sufficient reason as the common expression of all of this forms - every object is subordinate to the psr. an analysis of the notion of permanent: … an analysis of the dreams: … the world as will the world as representation the world as will criticism of the kantian philosophy qa what is the ontological nature of the idea of ‘will’? how does it relate with other deepest principle of reality? whatever underlies all reality at the deepest level — let’s call that will. a metaphysically rich total - but empirically empty. schopenhauer’s “will” is not an empirical hypothesis; it’s a metaphysical postulate . all the laws of nature and causal relations are manifestations of the will’s self-objectification at different levels. for example: - physical forces = will objectified in the lowest grade (gravity, magnetism, electricity). - biological life = higher grade of the same will manifesting as instinct and striving. - human consciousness = the will’s most reflective form, where it can become aware of itself. aspects: - ontologically: the will is the noumenal substrate of existence , the ultimate reality beneath all appearances. - epistemologically: it is known directly only through inner experience (our own willing). - cosmologically: it manifests as all forces, processes, and beings in the phenomenal world. - metaphysically: it replaces the idea of god or rational order with a blind, irrational, striving force. relation: principle schopenhauer’s relation to it --- --- reason / intellect a secondary tool of the will; evolved to serve its blind striving. matter the phenomenal manifestation of will — its “visibility.” form (space, time, causality) conditions of representation, not of the will itself; they structure appearance, not essence. being / becoming the will is being without becoming (it does not change); becoming occurs in its manifestations. unity / multiplicity the will is one; multiplicity belongs to its phenomenal appearances. comparison: system deepest principle character --- --- --- heraclitus logos dynamic order through conflict parmenides being eternal, unchanging one spinoza substance (deus sive natura) rational unity of attributes kant thing-in-itself unknown, beyond representation schopenhauer will non-rational, striving essence underlying all phenomena what does mean when we said “the world is my will”? saying ‘the world is my will’ is misleading; schopenhauer’s point is simply that ‘the world is will,’ and adding ‘my’ incorrectly ties it to personal subjectivity, which was not his intention as infer by the general used by schopenhauer used of the term will . how to validate the schopenhauer system? validation criterion description --- --- logical consistency check that propositions do not contradict each other. conceptual clarity core concepts should be well-defined and operationalizable. explanatory power system should explain phenomena coherently. systemic integration all parts of the system should form a unified worldview. comparative evaluation evaluate against other philosophical frameworks for robustness. practical coherence ethical and aesthetic prescriptions should follow logically from metaphysics. phenomenological plausibility insights should resonate with human experience. critical scrutiny examine for hidden assumptions, circular reasoning, or contradictions. is representation part of the grammar of representation? representation itself is the object the grammar governs, not the grammar itself — but understanding “representation” conceptually is necessary to describe the grammar. is representation the most abstract notion that there is? if we include representations of forms, structures, and elements in reality, then representation can be considered the most abstract notion, because it subsumes both the objects themselves and our perception or conceptualization of them. representation is not just a mirror of reality—it is the framework through which any element, form, or pattern can be encoded, understood, or related to other elements. how the idea of representation represent itself? representation can reflect upon itself: by analyzing its own structure and mechanisms, we can construct a meta-representation —a representation of representation. this is a self-referential process, where the concept both is and describes the act of representing. is time a notion of reality (a posteriori), or a notion of the mind (a priory)? what do we mean by a notion of reality? what do we mean by a notion of the mind? note: some notions begin as constructs of the mind but can later become part of reality, such as money, laws, or social institutions. some notions, such as time or causality, appear to exist on a continuum between objective reality and mental construct, rather than having a sharp boundary. is there a unifying grammar - representation + reality? … references - huge mistake of smith framework - it’s that he does not underlying the idea of the technique - and does not pay sufficiency attention to production. adam smith's critique of "mercantilism" is often directed at a constructed category rather than a coherent school of thought. what later became known as mercantilism encompassed a diverse collection of writers, administrators, merchants, and policymakers whose views frequently differed on important questions. as a result, it is often more informative to study figures such as thomas mun, josiah child, jean-baptiste colbert, and antonio serra individually rather than treating them as members of a unified doctrine. one recurring concern among many of these thinkers was the development of productive capacity, manufacturing, technical capabilities, and state-supported economic development , but beyond this there was considerable variation. a similar issue appears in the work of karl marx. like smith's use of "mercantilism," marx's concept of "capitalism" aggregates a vast range of institutions, historical arrangements, and economic systems under a single label. while marx emphasized production, technology, and the organization of labor, critics argue that this framework underemphasized the role of distributed coordination mechanisms—especially markets, price systems, entrepreneurship, and decentralized decision-making. in this view, both "mercantilism" and "capitalism" function partly as broad abstractions that can obscure significant differences among the historical systems and actors grouped under those terms. todo: the technical formulation of alternatives histories is called stochastic processes . a random sample path (random run) is the technical name for a succession of virtual historical events, starting at a given data and ending at another. what is a monte carlo generator? a computational mechanism that replicates the core statistical structure of selected aspects of reality, enabling the generation of random manifestations consistent with that structure. linear history assumption: hegelian teleology and related pseudoscientific doctrines that posit a necessary, unidirectional progression of history. when looking at the past you are basically looking at only one observation being realized - not seeing the others that did not - creating a false sense of determinism. a mistake is not something that should be evaluated after the fact; it can only be evaluated in light of the information known at the moment of the decision. randomness, nonsense, and scientific intellectual see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/fashionable nonsense. - literary text → can be generated stochastically; coherence is interpretive. - scientific text → is constrained by a theory; coherence is structural and explanatory. survival of the least fit – can evolution be fooled by randomness? the solution to this apparent dilemma is to understand philosophy as a bearer of our residual powers of insight: those that the specialized sciences fail to exhaust and that we identify with the imagination. two moves define the aspect of our mental experience that we call the imagination. the first move — the one emphasized by kant — is distancing from the phenomenon. the second move—which kant neglected — is the subsumption of the actual under a range of variations in the realm of the adjacent possibilities: what the actual can become next. ontology (as natural philosophy and social theory) in 1697 - leibniz “on the ultimate origin of things” introduce the doctrine of the “best of all possible worlds”. metaphysical rationalism: the principles underlying reality are logically necessary and intelligible a priori —that is, they can be known independently of experience. check this: leibniz - to complete our explanations, we cannot simply offer more causal inquiry. the philosophy of deep structure is the practice of trying to describe the deep structure of reality — a view that presupposes the existence of a deep structure in nature. the philosophy of deep structure has a problem explaining let’s say phase transition - or emergence - elements that can’t be explained in terms of the fundamental elements - and interactions. the other great answer to the question - what is the world like? speculative monism. speculative monism is the philosophical vision that reality is one, but this oneness is an active, self-articulating process — a unity that thinks, becomes, and differentiates within itself. what distinguishes speculative monism from deep structure philosophy ? speculative monism focuses on the unit of change , aiming to uncover the most fundamental structure or constituent of reality — the basic elements and their interactions that give rise to all phenomena. in india, the dominant principle guiding the investigation of reality was speculative monism — a view evident in the indic vedanta , the upanishads , and early buddhism . schopenhauer , with his idea of the will , was also a proponent of speculative monism . a via negativa definition is a way of defining something by stating what it is not rather than what it is . some extreme version of speculative monism - even denied time - which denied timed also. temporal naturalism, a third view into the deep principle of reality - the philosophy of change - even changes changes. what is natural history ? mathematics has been the most powerful instrument of natural science, the torch illuminating what otherwise seems impossible to retrieve from the shadows of the perceived world. but it also offers natural science a poisoned gift, the idea of timeless laws of nature. mathematics “explicates” by bringing out what is implicit in the conception of a structured whole or bundle of relations, stated in numerical or geometrical language. ❓ which are the limits of mathematics? does mathematical methods has a conception of time - that is, process? - mathematics does not model the structure of phenomena - just the relation between variables. ❓ which are the consequences of the ‘principle of non contradiction’ and time in logic? if time is central to what the world looks like, so it’s causality. causality captures some kind of temporal succession or influence. causality assumes time - and times assumes causality. causality unites moments in time. causation - presupposes time. a cause must precede an effect. causality is connection in time. the concept of causation should not be treated as binary (0 or 1); rather, it represents the strength of the connection between events. when roberto mention ontology - does he takes into account change as an ontic element - or just the ‘material substrate’? ontic formulations of nature are typically dualistic: (grace / nature), (mind / body), ( res cogitans / res extensa ), (things-in-themselves / things as they appear to us), etc. epistemology (as inquiry into inquiry) theory and program of inquiry. the human condition: becoming more human by becoming more godlike ethics (as clarity about the conduct of life) two ways to die only once the unresolved contest between the ethics of self-fashioning and the connection politics (as struggle over the future of society) politics: the program of deep freedom references - roberto mangabeira unger - https://www.bremontix.xyz/locus-instrumentorum/sociology/ - curiel, e. - mathematical induction - nondeterminism: … - performance - complexity: … - program execution: - lazy evaluation (demand driven): an evaluation strategy in which expressions or computations are only evaluated when they are needed. this allows computations on infinite data structures. - eager evaluation : … - programming strategies - higher order programming: uses of higher order constructs like higher order functions. - recursion is a strategy for defining a computation or data structure in terms of smaller instances of itself, along with a base case. the resulting construct is called a recursive computation or recursive data structure . - threads of computation (i have really good notes about this - bremontix ars) - concurrency - dataflow: what happens if we try to use a variable that hasn’t been bound yet? note: when studying a model of computation ask yourself: representation: how is the computational process formally described? - what structures encode inputs, outputs, and state (e.g., strings, graphs, functions) semantics: what do these representations mean? (2019). super thinking: the big book of mental models. penguin. @book{weinberg2019super, title={super thinking: the big book of mental models}, author={weinberg, gabriel and mccann, lauren}, year={2019}, publisher={penguin} } notes --- … index reading note(s) - “mental models” are not a new ontological kind — just a rhetorically convenient subset of mental representations focused on structure and analogy. - … mental model space - [conceptual descriptor] critical mass is a systemic threshold property — a condition marking the transition from one regime of behavior to another. signature variable, condition, emergent effect . - this is by not means a model - but it’s concept to denote a special value - that antecedent a transition in the regime of behavior of a system. - [inverse thinking - problem inversion] a technique (or metatechnique ) used by an agent to reformulate a problem space by inverting its guiding objective or constraints, in order to reveal alternative formulations, hidden assumptions, or neglected solution paths. - unforced error is a diagnostic concept — specifically, a type of agentic error that denotes a failure originating from the agent’s own actions or decisions , not from external pressures or uncontrollable conditions. a mistake that can be prevented - with high probability - again, not a model. - antifragility is a systemic property concept — a concept describing how a system responds to stressors, variability, or disorder - if a system get’s better when in stress then it’s antifragile . — again, not a model. 🧭 i. foundational cognitive concepts concept type description --- --- --- first principles thinking reasoning technique breaking complex problems into their fundamental truths and reasoning up from there. second-order thinking reasoning technique considering the downstream consequences of actions beyond the immediate effects. inversion (problem inversion) metatechnique reversing a problem’s formulation to expose hidden assumptions or failure modes. opportunity cost economic logic the true cost of any choice is the next best alternative forgone. confirmation bias cognitive bias tendency to favor information that confirms preexisting beliefs. availability heuristic cognitive bias overweighting information that is easily recalled. occam’s razor epistemic heuristic prefer the simplest explanation that fits the facts. hanlon’s razor diagnostic heuristic “never attribute to malice what can be explained by incompetence.” map–territory distinction epistemic concept models are representations, not the reality itself. circle of competence self-reflective concept operate within areas where one has deep understanding. ⚙️ ii. systems & process concepts concept type description --- --- --- feedback loops (positive/negative) systemic mechanism cyclic causal chains that amplify or stabilize system behavior. leverage points systemic concept locations in a system where a small change produces large effects. critical mass systemic property threshold beyond which system behavior qualitatively changes. bottlenecks structural constraint points limiting the throughput or performance of a system. diminishing returns functional relationship each additional input yields smaller marginal benefit. compounding growth mechanism reinforcement of gains over time through reinvestment. path dependence historical property early decisions constrain future options and trajectories. emergence systemic property complex behavior arising from simple local interactions. homeostasis adaptive mechanism system self-regulation to maintain stability. antifragility systemic property improving under stress, volatility, or randomness. 📊 iii. decision & optimization concepts concept type description --- --- --- expected value probabilistic evaluator weighting outcomes by probability and magnitude. bayesian updating epistemic mechanism revising beliefs based on new evidence. margin of safety risk management concept building buffers against uncertainty or error. regression to the mean statistical tendency extreme outcomes tend to revert toward the average. comparative advantage economic principle efficiency comes from specializing where relative advantage is highest. trade-offs decision concept every gain entails an associated cost elsewhere. sunk cost fallacy cognitive trap continuing a behavior due to prior investment. 🧩 iv. structural & organizational concepts concept type description --- --- --- incentive structures causal driver systems behave according to how participants are rewarded. principal–agent problem governance problem misalignment between decision-maker and beneficiary. tragedy of the commons collective dynamics shared resources overused when individual incentives misalign with collective welfare. network effects structural dynamic the value of a system increases with the number of participants. power laws distribution property a small number of causes produce a large proportion of effects. lindy effect temporal property the longer something has survived, the longer it’s expected to survive. scale economies production property efficiency increases with scale — until diseconomies set in. 🧠 v. learning, adaptation & error concepts concept type description --- --- --- iterative learning / trial and error adaptive mechanism knowledge accumulates through feedback from failure. unforced error diagnostic concept self-generated failure not caused by external conditions. cognitive dissonance psychological mechanism mental discomfort from holding contradictory beliefs. learning curve empirical relationship efficiency improves predictably with experience. mental models stack metacognitive concept interlinking models across domains for compound reasoning. meta-learning reflective concept learning about the structure and process of learning itself. 🪞 vi. philosophical & epistemic anchors concept type description --- --- --- chesterton’s fence conservatism principle don’t remove an existing rule before understanding why it exists. goodhart’s law measurement paradox “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” law of unintended consequences systemic insight interventions produce unforeseen secondary effects. correspondence vs. coherence theories of truth epistemic models competing conceptions of what it means for something to be “true.” is–ought gap (hume’s law) normative boundary you cannot derive moral prescriptions from factual statements. occasion–structure distinction systems-theoretic concept behavior emerges from the interaction of structure and occasion. being wrong less anything than can wrong, will spend your time wisely becoming one with nature lies, dammed lies, and statistics decisions, decisions dealing with conflict unlocking people’s potential flex your market power

documents.title: Zhirkov, I. (2017). Low-Level Programming. Springer.
documents.text: zhirkov, i. (2017). low-level programming. springer. @book{zhirkov2017low, title={low-level programming}, author={zhirkov, igor}, year={2017}, publisher={springer} } notes --- note: this book covers only the intel 64 architecture. index assembly language and computer architecture basic computer architecture the term “model of computation” is defined as the set of primitive “operations → computation” and their cost. the term “model of computation” will also be used to denote “an abstract machine” - that is a model of a computer - what is can do and how does it do it. - this will not be treated in this book. von newman architecture: a computational architecture in which program instructions and data share the same memory space , are represented in the same addressable format, and are fetched sequentially through a unified bus. the cpu operates using a fetch–decode–execute cycle , retrieving both instructions and operands from main memory, which creates the characteristic von neumann bottleneck : system throughput is constrained by the bandwidth of the memory–cpu channel. image.png the assembly language for a given processor is a set of mnemonics that correspond to the machine code — the binary-encoded instructions executed by the hardware. intel 64 architecture aka intel 64 system model. category part description --- --- --- execution core general-purpose registers (gprs) rax, rbx, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, rbp, rsp, r8–r15; integer arithmetic, pointers, stack, calling conventions. instruction pointer (rip) address of the next instruction to execute; updated automatically by control-flow instructions. rflags condition codes (zf, cf, of…), control bits, system flags. simd/vector registers xmm0–31, ymm0–31, zmm0–31 for sse/avx/avx-512 floating-point & vector operations. floating-point stack (x87 fpu) eight 80-bit fp registers in stack form; legacy but still architecturally present. segment registers cs, ds, es, ss, fs, gs; hold segment base/cache; mostly flat in 64-bit mode except fs/gs base. control & privilege control registers cr0/cr2/cr3/cr4/cr8; enable paging, protection, system features, tlb behavior. model-specific registers (msrs) per-core configuration registers for apic, power, performance monitoring, syscall, etc. privilege levels (rings) four privilege rings (0–3); os kernel in ring 0, user apps in ring 3. system call interface syscall/sysret, sysenter/sysexit; transitions between user and kernel mode. interrupts & exceptions interrupt descriptor table (idt) table of gate descriptors for hardware interrupts, traps, faults, nmis. apic / x2apic local apic + ioapic for interrupt routing, timers, ipi, vector assignment. fault handling page faults, gp faults, protection faults, fp exceptions, debug traps. debug state dr0–dr7 registers; breakpoints and single-step state. memory system virtual memory 4-level or 5-level paging (pml4/pdpt/pd/pt); 48–57-bit virtual addresses. page tables hierarchical translation structures referenced by cr3; cached in tlb. hardware stack stack pointer (rsp), call/return operations, red zone, shadow stack (cet). memory protection paging, supervisor/user bits, nx bit, memory-type boundaries. translation & coherency tlb (translation lookaside buffer) caches virtual→physical translations; separate l1 dtlb, itlb, unified l2 tlb. memory ordering tso (total store order) with fences (lfence, sfence, mfence); reordering rules. cache coherency protocol mesi/moesi implemented in hardware across cores. paging & ept hardware-assisted virtualization (extended page tables) for vms. cache hierarchy l1 caches per-core: l1i (instructions), l1d (data), lowest latency. l2 cache private per core; larger, slower than l1. l3 cache shared among cores; last-level cache (llc). cache line fundamental unit of coherency and movement (typically 64 bytes). branching & speculation branch predictor btb, bpu, indirect predictors; reduce control hazards. speculative execution execution before resolution of branches/memory dependencies. reorder buffer (rob) tracks speculative instructions for in-order retirement. micro-op cache caches decoded µops to bypass instruction decode. microarchitecture pipeline fetch unit retrieves instructions (speculatively). decode unit decodes complex x86 instructions into µops. reservation stations dispatching and scheduling of µops to execution units. execution units alus, fpus, vector units, agus, crypto units, etc. retirement unit commits architectural state after speculation clears. system & power power management c-states, p-states; turbo boost control. performance monitoring pmcs, pebs, lbrs; used by profilers (perf, vtune, tracy). rdt / qos resource partitioning of caches and memory bandwidth. assembly language legacy virtual memory compilation pipeline interrupts and systems calls models of computation the c programming language basics type system code structure memory syntax, semantics, and pragmatics good code practices between c and assembly translation details shared objects and code models performance multithreading appendices using gdb using make system calls performance test information references - …

(1989). asia’s next giant: south korea and late industrialization. oxford university press. @misc{amsden1989asia, title={asia’s next giant: south korea and late industrialization}, author={amsden, alice h}, year={1989}, publisher={oxford university press} } notes --- a book about a ' late industrializer ': south korea. the term 'late industrialization' began to appear in the english language around 1900. index industrializing thought learning financial profile of south korea. korea differs from most other later industrializing countries is in the discipline its state exercises over private firms . invest now in inhouse technological capability, even if outside expertise is cheaper, to reap the rewards of self reliance later. park chung hee : book “the country, the revolution, and i”. - which was the incentive system? - how companies were evaluated? - how the financial sector was structure? government was basically the only banker. - how the entering into new industries was organized? - how the capital account was organized? did capital flight happens? - how the process of “technological learning“ was organized? - was fdi allow? - how korean firms managed to get technical know-how? the state and business: history and policies … a history of backwardness this chapter is about how korea with weak and incapable institutions undertake industrialization. japan force korea to free trade from 1876 to 1945 . the socio-political structure of joseon korea (also known as yi dynasty korea ) was a rigid confucian hierarchy where the ruling elite, known as the yangban , held significant power over politics, land, and social privileges, while commoners ( sangmin ) and lower classes like slaves ( cheonmin ) had limited rights and were bound by strict social stratification that emphasized loyalty, duty, and obedience to authority. this balance between the monarchy and aristocracy create stability; but make structural change hard to happens. how to characterize south korea feudal society? japanese rule: - end slavery - introduce a civil code - … - japanese rule disrupted korea's emerging foundations for modernization without establishing meaningful new ones. - by the end of japanese colonial rule , korean society was deeply fractured and unable to sustain itself, with peasants clashing against landlords and anti-colonial resisters opposing collaborators. under these conditions, the machinery of modern governance that japan had established became a paradoxically valuable, if contentious, legacy. cold war: - korean war; the new north and south korea. - thesis: how the new korea state beurocracy was recycle from the old state hood class the yangban. aid and the origins of diversified business groups: - aid and corruption by syngman rhee. - in 1948-1960 a set of well connected business people were give a lot of access of foreign reserves; and local market, …, subsidized loans, a whole class of privileges; this created the first ‘diversified business groups’ (at the moments commercial and basic production gans one should say); some of the industries where ‘textiles, paper, housing, mining, fertilizer, flour, alcohol, glass, pottery, livestock, construction, and …’ - … views on the feature of korea in the late 1950: - the students - the united states - the military the abcs of japanese and korean accumulation how korea rise to be an export country. do less developed countries require greater intervention ? the emergence of international division of labor . origins and evolution of global value and supply chains? table of growth by sectors … japan textiles trade with china; how japan overtake the uk ? kysongsong spinning and weaving company founded in 1919 was probability the first capitalistic enterprise in korea. by 1965 exports were a firm idea in park toolbox. “state of the nation message” on january 16, 1965. study on exports targets. hubbard on the competitiveness of japanese textiles : - wage almost makes no different; - group control over the industry by japan cotton spinners association and various other trade association in order to check overproduction and uneconomic competition. - large and integrated manufacturing units, working two shifts a day and equipped with ring spindles [the most modern technology] and, to considerable extend, also with automatic looms. - shipping subsidies and low shipping cost. - concentration of raw-cotton imports in the hands of a large few trading concerns, and the system of bulk purchase whereby by spinners if often able to obtain his raw cotton at the lowest possible cost. - concentration of raw-cotton imports in the hands of a few large trading concerns, and the system of bulk purchase, whereby the spinner if often able to obtain his raw cotton at the lowest possible cost. - great efficiency in marketing the finished product resulting from the maintenance of closer contact with the customers, and from intimate cooperation between the manufacturing and mercantile sections of the industry. - [added] the quality of japanese management? where does the management culture of japan came from? japanese exports markets: - the preponderance of japanese manufactured exports was destined not for more but still for less industrialized countries. - japan was sufficiency industrialized by 1920 and 1930 to pursue a “beggar-thy-neighbor” exchange rate policy to expand its exports, against the wishes of the advanced countries, which wanted an appreciated yen . - japan economy before world war ii was sui generis , combining great modernity and backwardness at the same time. - … korea textiles 1950-1960…: - overcapacity, - weak foreign marketing channels, - tarrifs in the us, - … exchange rates: - many exchange rates to favor exporters, - … investment policy: - … the dynamics of growth … late industrialization is characterized by three facets of growth, as korea exemplifies. - the first relates to diversification, or entrepreneurial decisions penetration of new industries, which ones to penetrate, when, and with that size investment. - the second relates to stabilization, or short-run macroeconomic policies to maintain the level of economic activity. - the third relates to the growth momentum itself. once under way, growth gains a momentum whose properties are distinct, depending on the presence or absence of new technological discoveries. ☑️ the spiraling of market power … getting relative prices “wrong”: a summary professional management of human resources the rise salaried engineers: automobile manufacturing the paradox of “unlimited” labor and rising wages the boom in education the dynamics of dynamic comparative advantage the switch in industrial leadership the world’s largest shipbuilder the triumph of steel from learner to teacher references - veblen, t., & mayer, o. g. (2017). monotonicity types. https://infoscience.epfl.ch/handle/20.500.14299/141536 @misc{item a9e12d1f1ccc4f599a04807162724c8a, title={monotonicity types}, url={https://infoscience.epfl.ch/handle/20.500.14299/141536}, abstractnote={in the face of the increasing trend in application development to interact with more and more remote services, and cognizant of the fact that issues arising from data consistency and task coordination are core challenges in distributed programming, the systems and data management communities have taken a keen interest in developing eventually consistent coordination-free models of distributed programming. these efforts have a striking similarity; they can all be characterized by the use of monotone functions as fundamental primitives of composition as well as the monotonic evolution of data over time. yet, ensuring that application code conforms to the monotonicity constraints of these programming models is a tricky and manual affair, without support from the underlying language or system. in this paper, we present monotonicity types, a language and type system for proving functions monotone, which we believe could enable the customization and extension of this class of distributed programming models. we provide a full formalization of monotonicity types, including a novel operational semantics oriented from the perspective inside of a function, as well as a type soundness proof using logical relations.}, author={clancy, kevin and miller, heather and meiklejohn, christopher}, year={2017}, keywords={crdts eventual consistency distributed computing concurrency types} } notes --- … references - https://infoscience.epfl.ch/entities/publication/a9e12d1f-1ccc-4f59-9a04-807162724c8a - https://prl.khoury.northeastern.edu/blog/2017/10/22/monotonicity-types-towards-a-type-system-for-eventual-consistency/

- … terminology note: we need to research on how freud uses these terms. psyche : the totality of the human mind, encompassing conscious and unconscious processes , thoughts, emotions, desires, and personality. psychoanalysis: a specific theoretical and therapeutic approach founded by sigmund freud that seeks to understand and resolve unconscious conflicts underlying thoughts, emotions, and behaviors through methods such as free association, dream analysis, interpretation of defense mechanisms, and transference work. neurosis : a mental or emotional disorder in which a person experiences chronic distress, anxiety, or maladaptive behaviors without a loss of reality testing . unlike psychosis, the person remains aware of reality but struggles to manage internal conflicts, impulses, or stress. - note this is a dead-term in modern “psychiatry” - in order to describe mental disorders . dream: … paper claim: every neurosis as its results - force out the patient of life - an alienating of him from reality - the loos of the ‘function of reality’. claim: the concept of repression gives insight into the genesis of neurosis. claim: neurotics turn away from reality because they find it unbearable - either the whole or parts of it. (reader - this has to an instance of a bad explanation). claim: unconscious mental processes—the residuals of early developmental phases—are governed by the primary processes, whose purpose is regulated by the pleasure-unpleasure principle, or more simply, the pleasure principle . claim: the main chooses to maintain (not dreams) or alterations of reality - it chooses to maintain what’s reality - and this is the reality principle . the paper introduces a description of attention and memory. the economic principle: … qa what’s the key of the paper? it describes consequences of the adaption to the reality principle; how the mind balances the reality - and pleasure principle. how do pleasure principle and reality principle interact? what freud explains using the pleasure principle and reality principle? what form of explanation is this? … references - https://tcf-website-media-library.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/20131846/formulations-on-the-two-principles-of-mental-functioning-sigmund-freud-1911.pdf - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/neurosis

documents.text: hume, d. (2016). an inquiry concerning human understanding (pp. 183–276). routledge. @incollection{hume2016enquiry, title={an enquiry concerning human understanding}, author={hume, david}, pages={183--276}, year={2016}, publisher={routledge} } notes --- note: david hume's enquiry is a refined version of his earlier treatise of human nature , presenting his empiricist philosophy in a more accessible way. qa: - what is the problem of induction? - what is the hume’s theory of causation? index publishers’ preface … autobiography … letter from adam smith to william strahan … author’s advertisement … of the different species of philosophy … - moral philosophy the science of human nature - branches of philosophy - [hedonismo] philosophers that considers man as born for action; and influenced in his measures by taste sentiment; there is no framework for light; just incentives. - [ascetismo / estoicismo / deontologismo] philosophers considers man in the light of a reasonable rather than an active being, and endeavor to form his understanding more than cultivate his manners. a set of philosophers trying to find the right framework for human life. - → ? a mixed - … of the origin of ideas impressions: lively, vivid perceptions (e.g., sensations, emotions) from direct experience. ideas: faint copies of impressions, formed in thought or memory. principle of copying: all ideas derive from prior impressions ("no idea without an antecedent impression"). association of ideas: ideas connect via three natural principles: - resemblance (e.g., a portrait reminds you of a person). - contiguity (e.g., thinking of a school leads to memories of classmates). - cause/effect (e.g., seeing lightning makes you expect thunder). simple vs. complex ideas - simple ideas : basic units (e.g., "red," "sweet") copied directly from impressions. - complex ideas : combinations of simple ideas (e.g., a "golden mountain" = gold + mountain). critique of abstract ideas - hume follows berkeley in rejecting innate or abstract ideas (e.g., "justice" is just a collection of related impressions). of the association of ideas … sceptical doubts concerning the operations of the understanding … sceptical solution of these doubts … of probability … of the idea of necessary connexion … of liberty and necessity … of the reason of animals … of miracles … of a particular providence and of a future state … of the academical or sceptical philosophy … references - https://archive.org/details/enquiryconcernin01hume/page/n9/mode/2up - david hume - https://davidhume.org/teaching/documents/hume notes copy principle.pdf

(2009). organizations: social systems conducting experiments. springer-verlag berlin heidelberg. @misc{jan2009organizations, title={organizations: social systems conducting experiments}, author={jan, achterbergh and dirk, vriens}, year={2009}, publisher={springer-verlag berlin heidelberg} } notes --- organizations as social systems conducting experiments & principles to design it. epistemological strategy : use the ‘posterior analytics’ strategy of aristotle (phonemena → data(endoxa) → key features (archai)). later use the archai to build a theory. index introducing organizations as social systems conducting experiments in this book we model organizations as organizations as social systems conducting experiments with their survival. in this chapter we expand on this idea; we elaborate on principles for the design of organizations, enabling them to survive; to continue conducting experiments . aristotle seeks to penetrate the essence of phenomena, examining their fundamental characteristics—elements that can only be negated if the entire phenomenon itself is negated. observations → strategy formulation by a group of managers : the director of the enterprise discusses a vision for the expansion of the enterprise in foreign markets, a social activity in which departments/heads of departments communicate and reason together to create new goals for the org ; a critical task because it affects the survival probability of the org. → a worker in trouble : a worker with work accumulated (several circumstances, machine failures, personal ill, etc.); the boss is pressing and has to communicate to realize its goals. usually, disturbances and regulatory actions are made to solve these issues. there are two ways: top-down (thinking about how things can go wrong and taking action to fix it) and giving the worker the tools to resolve the disturbances (autoregulation) … organisations archai → experimental character : make decisions regarding objectives, implement innovative regulatory actions to overcome disruptions, and achieve these goals, → social systemic character : interactions, expectations, and communication by a set of people that define a group (organization) with a standard set of goals; models and theories. - ❓ what is physics far from equilibrium? - ❓ in the evoltion line of a simple - complex system; how relevant is information storage? - ❓ how small is a 1nm? how many of such elements in one squared milimeter? - ❓ what is the range of scales of viruses? 20 - 30nm in diameter. - ❓ what is the range of viruses genomes? - ❓ how many proteins does covid-19 performs? - ❓ what is gene regulation? - ❓ how can we capture a ic and not a virus (vastly smaller in components)? reflect more on page 6 [virus vs ic]. - ... index introduction the complex world complexity science is about how systems are different from physics and chemistry; but dependent on them (all reality is). all systems obeys the laws of physics and chemistry - but describing only in terms of those basic laws seems imposible. open: implies positioned whthing a chemical or electrochemical gradient. self-organizing: refers to rules amplifying fluctuations into coordinated space-time patterns. dissipative: refers to dynamics that are irreversable and that braek time-reversal symetry. uncertain: describes an open-ended space of possible states not enumerable in initial conditions, adaptive: describes the capture of information by a system from environment that promotes persistance and increases multiplicy. teleology: rfers to a goal-oriented explanation, interpreting structures or dynamics in terms of their functions. note: complexity is really a paradigm; it can not be reduced to a set of techniques; and it does not apply to every system; only to those in which reductionist techniques fall short. two main types of systems: - a: closed, reversible, symetry-dominated, and predictable classical domains (aka reductionism apply), - b: open, self-organizing, dissipative, uncertain, and adaptive domains are the subject of this book (aka reducctionism does not apply). descriptions: - a: great regularities; that give rise to short descriptions, and few initial conditions. - b: emergent regularities; constructed from "contigent histories" ???, describe using coarse-grained rules and nested boundaries conditions. systems spectrums: - [equilibruim] - [non equilibrium and self organizing] - [self adaptative self synthesizing organizations with long evolutioary histories]. origins of the complexity paradigm: a new paradigm will emerge; when the old stop working (it's can explain new datasets of interest). - new games; new rules: science does not merely the process of fitting new data into old models or a constellation of them; is only creating new ones to feet the data; sinse the old ones are not capable.. - hermeneutics: in order to understand the parts we need the whole; in order to understand the whole we need the parts (chikend-egg problem). constructing the complexity paradigm: - new paradigms are creating by a combination of new phenomena, new methods, re-organization / unifications of fields. - complexity is an integrative
